title: Baseline retest for cores/bench
Replace combinational 32-bit divider with a multi-cycle iterative divider that stalls EX
motivation:
The baseline's worst path is 199.8 ns (Fmax 5.44 MHz, 156 logic cells):
forward_unit -> EX operand mux -> alu.sv -> BRAM address. The cell count and
depth point at the combinational `/` and `%` operators in alu.sv (signed DIV,
unsigned DIVU, signed REM, unsigned REMU), each a 32-stage subtract array.
That one cone costs thousands of LUT4s and fixes the clock period of the
whole core. The other EX-stage logic (adder, shifter, comparators, DSP
multiplier) is several times shorter. CoreMark does not execute integer
divides in its timed loop, because the compiler turns divides by constants
into multiplies and the matrix, list and state kernels contain none. Divide
latency therefore costs almost no iterations/cycle, while removing the
divider from the combinational cone can raise Fmax several-fold. Fitness is
iter/cycle x Fmax, so this is nearly free Fmax.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU out of alu.sv into a new rtl/divider.sv, a radix-2
shift-subtract iterative divider that takes roughly 34-36 cycles. EX stalls
on a divide the same way the pipeline already stalls on dmem backpressure.

1. New rtl/divider.sv with ports clock, reset, start, is_signed, want_rem,
   a, b, busy, done, result. Per-cycle logic is a 33-bit subtract plus a
   mux; a registered result is presented in the DONE state. Operands are
   latched on start (taken from the post-forward rs1/rs2 values), because
   ID/EX's rs values and the forwarding selects go stale after about two
   cycles.
   - Signed ops: take abs() of the operands while latching, run the unsigned
     restoring loop, then negate in a dedicated FIXUP cycle into a result
     register. Negate the quotient if sign(a)^sign(b) and b != 0; negate the
     remainder if sign(a).
   - Divide by zero: the unsigned loop gives quotient 0xFFFFFFFF and
     remainder = dividend, matching RV32M. Suppress the quotient negation
     when b == 0 so signed DIV by 0 stays -1.
   - INT_MIN / -1: abs(INT_MIN) = 0x80000000 as unsigned, so the quotient is
     0x80000000 after negation and the remainder is 0, as required.
   - Keep the original rs1/rs2 in extra regs (RVFI-only, so they are pruned
     from the timed netlist) so the retiring EX/MEM record carries correct
     rs1_val/rs2_val.

2. rtl/ex_stage.sv:
   - Compute div_op = in.valid && alu_op in {DIV, DIVU, REM, REMU}, wrapped in
     `ifndef RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS`. Under ALTOPS div_op is tied to 0 and the
     existing alu.sv xor-of-sub stand-ins are used unchanged, so riscv-formal
     behaves as before.
   - New output `div_stall` = div_op && !div_done. The divider FSM
     (IDLE -> RUN x32 -> FIXUP -> DONE) advances only when !stall (the
     existing dmem stall), so a dmem stall freezes it consistently.
   - While div_stall is high, the EX/MEM register captures a bubble
     (reg_q <= '0, valid=0, reg_write=0, mem ops=0), unless stall (dmem) is
     holding it. In the DONE cycle EX/MEM captures the divider result via
     `alu_result = div_op ? div_result : alu_result_comb` along with the
     normal instr/pc/rd fields, and the FSM returns to IDLE.
   - A divide is neither a branch nor a jump, so redirect stays 0 while it
     sits in EX.

3. rtl/hazard_unit.sv and rtl/core.sv: add a `div_stall` input to the
   hazard unit.
     stall_if = ... || div_stall
     stall_id = ... || div_stall
   flush_id is unchanged, since load_use and redirect are both 0 while a
   divide is in EX. stall_ex_mem and hold_mem_wb are unchanged; the bubble
   injected into EX/MEM during the divide ripples to MEM/WB with valid=0, so
   no RVFI retirement occurs and rvfi_order stays +1 per retirement. Forwarding
   is unaffected: the bubble has rd=0 and reg_write=0, and the instruction
   behind the divide forwards from EX/MEM in the normal way after DONE.

4. rtl/alu.sv: delete the `/` and `%` expressions from the non-ALTOPS branch
   (DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU fall to `default: out = 0`). Keep the ALTOPS branch
   byte-for-byte. MUL/MULH/MULHU/MULHSU stay combinational and unchanged. The
   DSP multiplier then becomes the next critical path, which should be much
   shorter than the divider cone.

5. Tests: remove the DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU vectors from test/test_alu.py (the ALU
   no longer implements them). Add test/test_divider.py driving divider.sv
   with the same vectors (by-zero, INT_MIN/-1, signs) plus a few hundred
   random cases against a Python reference. Add one pipeline-level case to
   test_pipeline.py: a DIV followed by a dependent ADD, checking the
   retirement order and rd_wdata.

Latency cost is about 35 extra cycles per executed divide. CoreMark's timed
loop has essentially none, so iter/cycle is unchanged to within noise, while
Fmax is limited by the next-longest path (multiplier or forward -> ALU ->
BRAM address) instead of the divider. LUT4 count also drops sharply (target
is under 10000; baseline 12312), which eases placement and routing.

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-001-r1s0 (improvement, +729.79%): Fmax is set by the single longest combinational cone, and the `/` `%` divider array in alu.sv was that cone (199.8 ns baseline path), so moving DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU into a multi-cycle divider that stalls EX (bubbles into EX/MEM, operands latched on start) gained far more Fmax than the ~35-cycle divide latency cost, because CoreMark's timed loop has no integer divides; look for other rarely-executed, deep ops to take off the critical path the same way.

title: Pull MUL/DIV out of the combinational ALU into a multi-cycle EX-stage unit
motivation:
The baseline closes timing at only 5.44 MHz. The worst path (199.8 ns, 156
logic cells, ~150 LUT levels) runs MEM/WB.rd -> forward_unit -> EX fwd mux ->
alu.sv -> BSRAM address, i.e. through the purely combinational SystemVerilog
`/` and `%` (four 32-bit dividers: DIV, DIVU, REM, REMU) and three 32x32->64
multipliers that sit inside the ALU result mux. Those operators also account
for most of the 12.3k LUT4. Every other EX path (fwd mux -> 32-bit add/shift
-> result mux, or fwd mux -> compare -> redirect -> PC mux) is an order of
magnitude shorter, so Fmax is set almost entirely by logic that CoreMark
barely executes: the timed region has essentially zero divides (the only
`%` is `% 65536`, which the compiler lowers to an AND; the real divisions
are in untimed init/report code), and only ~1-2k multiplies per iteration
(matrix_mul_const / mul_vect / mul_matrix / bitextract) out of ~449k cycles
per iteration. Paying a few extra cycles per MUL and ~34 per DIV costs about
1-2% in cycles/iteration while removing the dominant critical path.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move all M-extension arithmetic out of alu.sv into a new sequential
`rtl/muldiv.sv` that the EX stage waits on, so alu.sv contains only
single-cycle ops (add/sub/logic/slt/shift/lui) and the critical path becomes
the ordinary forward -> add/shift -> EX/MEM path (expected Fmax well above
50 MHz instead of 5.4 MHz; the multicycle ops add ~2% CPI).

1. New module rtl/muldiv.sv (clock, reset, start, op[4:0], a, b, advance;
   outputs done, result[31:0], a_q, b_q). On the first cycle an M-op is in EX
   (start = ex_is_md && idle && !done) it latches the *forwarded* rs1/rs2 and
   op into a_q/b_q/op_q, so no later cycle depends on forwarding (the
   forwarding sources have moved on by then). The unit then runs from
   registers only:
   - MUL/MULH/MULHU/MULHSU: sign-extend both operands to 33 bits (signedness
     flags per op), split into a 16-bit low half and a signed 17-bit high
     half, and form the four partial products p_ll, p_lh, p_hl, p_hh with
     <=17x17 signed `*` (maps to MULT18X18 DSPs, which the baseline already
     uses). Cycle A: register the four products. Cycle B: register
     p_ll + ((p_lh+p_hl)<<16) + (p_hh<<32) (split into two cycles if this
     shows up on the critical path); then done=1 with result = low 32 bits
     for MUL or high 32 bits for MULH*. Total ~4 cycles in EX (3 bubbles).
   - DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU: iterative radix-2 restoring divider on |a|,|b|
     (32 iterations, one 32-bit subtract+compare per cycle), then a sign-fix
     cycle. Divide-by-zero falls out of the unsigned algorithm (q = all ones,
     r = |a|); the signed fix-up must NOT negate q when b==0 (DIV by 0 must
     return 0xFFFFFFFF) and negates r by the sign of a (so REM by 0 = a).
     INT_MIN / -1 falls out naturally (q = 0x80000000 after negation, r = 0).
     ~35 cycles; irrelevant for CoreMark since the timed region has ~0 divides.
   done stays high (result held) until `advance`, which is asserted when the
   M-op leaves EX: advance = ex_is_md && done && !stall_ex_mem. advance
   returns the unit to IDLE so the next instruction in ID/EX can start in its
   first EX cycle.

2. ex_stage.sv: ex_is_md = in.valid && in.ctrl.alu_op >= ALU_MUL (decoder
   only emits alu_op 11..18 for legal M R-types, bubbles are ALU_ADD).
   ex_wait = ex_is_md && !md_done. alu_result into EX/MEM is
   ex_is_md ? md_result : alu_out. While ex_wait && !stall: EX/MEM captures a
   bubble (reg_q <= '0, valid=0, reg_write=0 so nothing forwards from it)
   instead of the instruction; the dmem-stall `hold` branch keeps priority.
   For RVFI correctness (cosim and riscv-formal compare rs1_rdata/rs2_rdata)
   reg_q.rs1_val / rs2_val must take a_q / b_q (the latched operands) when
   the M-op completes, not the forwarding-mux outputs of the final cycle;
   those fields only feed RVFI so this costs no timed logic.

3. hazard_unit.sv / core.sv: add input ex_wait; stall_if |= ex_wait and
   stall_id |= ex_wait (PC and ID/EX hold, IF/ID is re-presented
   combinationally exactly like the existing load-use case). flush_id,
   flush_if and redirect logic are unchanged: an M-op in EX is never a
   branch/jump/load, so redirect and load-use cannot be active in the same
   cycle, and flush_id already yields to dmem_stall. Older instructions
   drain through MEM/WB normally while the bubbles flow behind them; an
   M-op's result is forwarded EX/MEM -> EX and MEM/WB -> EX through the
   existing forward_unit with no changes. dmem_stall while an M-op waits or
   is done simply holds EX/MEM and ID/EX (advance is gated by
   !stall_ex_mem, and the unit's operands/result are registered).

4. Formal/ALTOPS: under `ifdef RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS` keep the existing
   (a+b)^K / (a-b)^K substitutions in alu.sv and force ex_is_md = 0 so the
   formal build has single-cycle M-ops exactly as today (a 35-cycle divide
   would not fit the 20-step BMC depth). The real (non-ALTOPS) branch uses
   muldiv.sv. Invariant 5b stays enforced by cocotb + cosim (and
   `make formal-deep`).

5. Tests: alu.sv no longer implements M ops in the real build, so move the
   MUL/MULH/MULHU/MULHSU/DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU vectors from test_alu.py into a
   new clocked test/test_muldiv.py (pulse start with op/a/b, wait for done
   with a <=40-cycle timeout, compare the result; keep the by-zero, INT_MIN/-1
   and back-to-back-divide cases) and add "muldiv.sv" to its run_cocotb
   sources. test_alu.py keeps only base-op tests. Run test_pipeline.py and
   cosim: M-op / dependent-op / load-then-M-op / dmem-stall-during-M-op
   sequences are the main places a hold/forwarding bug would show.

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-002-r1s1 (regression, +710.23%): After the divider was already moved out (hyp-001: 45.2 MHz, 2467 LUT4), the critical path became the 27 ns regfile -> ID -> EX compare/forward -> redirect -> PC mux (22 levels) and the 32x32 multipliers were already on DSPs, so also moving MUL/MULH* into a multi-cycle muldiv.sv could not shorten the limiting path and only added ~3 EX bubbles per multiply plus an ex_wait term in stall_if/stall_id, netting slightly below hyp-001 (98.20 vs 100.57); re-read the new critical path after each fix and target redirect/forward/PC logic rather than the next-largest arithmetic block.

title: Zero-bubble fetch-stage BTB (32-entry, 2-bit counters) validated by predicted-next-PC compare in EX
motivation:
The core has no branch prediction: every taken branch, JAL and JALR resolves in EX and
redirects the PC, discarding the one wrong-path fetch behind it (exactly 1 bubble per
taken control-flow instruction; not-taken branches are free). Measured on the actual
CoreMark ELF (2K, -O3) with the Verilator cosim retirement trace: 2,937,037 retired
instructions, 4,514,348 cycles (CPI 1.54) under the 22% imem+dmem stall model, of which
532k are conditional branches (296k taken), 49.6k JAL and 13.8k JALR -> 359k taken
control-flow instructions = 8.0% of all cycles are redirect bubbles. Only 341 distinct
static sites ever redirect, and the hottest 16 / 32 / 64 sites cover 70% / 83% / 93% of
the dynamic redirects, so a small BTB captures most of it. The Fmax critical path is
the combinational mul/div ALU (~200 ns, forward_unit -> ALU -> EX/MEM) while the
fetch/redirect logic is a few tens of ns, so a predictor adds IPC essentially for free in
timing terms. A static ID-stage scheme cannot help here because decode already happens in
the IF cycle (the IF/ID bundle is combinational) -- only a PC-indexed fetch-time
predictor can remove the bubble.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a small direct-mapped branch target buffer to if_stage, read combinationally with the
current PC, so a predicted-taken branch/jump steers the NEXT fetch with zero bubbles.
Correctness is guaranteed by construction rather than by trusting the BTB: the predicted
next PC (pred_next[31:2]) travels with the instruction in the ID/EX register, and EX
compares it with the architectural next PC (the existing pc_next expression: misalign ->
pc+4, jump -> jump_target, taken branch -> branch_target, else pc+4). EX raises `redirect`
iff in.valid && actual_next[31:2] != in.pred_next, and redirects to actual_next. This
subsumes the current redirect logic (an unpredicted taken branch/jump mispredicts because
pred_next = pc+4), and makes aliased, stale or wrong-kind BTB hits (even on non-branch
instructions) harmless: they cost the same 1-cycle redirect the baseline pays. RVFI
pc_wdata still comes from the architectural pc_next, so riscv-formal and cosim see
identical retirement streams. flush_if / flush_id / stall logic in hazard_unit is
unchanged (it keys off `redirect`).

BTB organisation: 32 entries direct-mapped, index = pc[6:2], entry = {valid, 6-bit tag
pc[12:7], target[19:2] (18 bits; upper target bits come from the current PC[31:20] since
all code is below 1 MiB -- a wrong guess is caught by the EX compare), 2-bit saturating
counter}. Predict taken iff valid && tag match && ctr[1]. next_pc = redirect ?
redirect_target : pred_taken ? {pc[31:20], target, 2'b00} : pc+4. The IF/ID bundle and
ID/EX register gain pred_next[31:2], pred_hit and pred_ctr[1:0] (bubbles/NOPs carry
pc+4, valid=0 so they never mispredict). To keep the BTB a single-write-port /
single-async-read-port array (maps to Gowin distributed RAM instead of ~900 flops), EX
does not re-read the BTB: it uses the pred_hit/pred_ctr carried with the instruction.
Update fires from EX when in.valid && !stall_ex_mem (so a branch held under a dmem stall
updates once) and the instruction is a branch or jump (is_branch|is_jump): actual taken
(actual_next != pc+4) -> if pred_hit write {valid, tag, actual_next, ctr+1 saturating},
else allocate with ctr=2'b10; not taken and pred_hit -> write ctr-1 (saturating at 0,
keep target/tag). JALR uses the same mechanism (last-target prediction).

Evidence from a Python model of exactly this scheme replayed over the real CoreMark
retirement trace (idealised: counted as 1 cycle per mispredict, update latency
ignored): 16 entries 6.6% fewer cycles, 32 entries 7.2%, 64 entries 7.3%, 256 entries
7.5%; 1-bit counters are ~0.6% worse than 2-bit; 2-way associativity adds <0.3%. So 32
direct-mapped entries sits at the knee of the curve (mispredicts drop from 359k to 58k).
The new EX-side 30-bit compare sits on redirect -> PC / flush, far shorter than the ALU
divide path, so Fmax should be unchanged (within P&R noise); area cost is a few hundred
LUTs plus ~33 extra ID/EX flops.

title: Prune the redirect cone: take EX redirect out of the IF->ID instruction/load-use path and narrow ID/EX flush fanout
motivation:
After the iterative divider (hyp-001-r1s0) the worst path is 27 ns / 22 LUT
levels: ID/EX operand register -> EX forward mux + compare/adder -> redirect
-> u_if -> u_hazard -> u_id -> u_if -> pc[31]. The module sequence shows the
late `redirect` signal fanning back out through if_stage's NOP mask
(`instr = (flush||redirect) ? NOP : imem_data`), into the hazard unit's
load-use compare (it reads if_id_w.instr[19:15]/[24:20]) and from there into
stall_if/stall_id/flush_id and the PC enable. That is a false path:
load-use needs a LOAD in ID/EX while redirect needs a BRANCH/JAL/JALR in
ID/EX, so the two can never be 1 together, and the PC mux already gives
redirect priority over stall. The tools cannot see this, so redirect's
timing is stacked in front of a 5-bit XOR compare, an AND/OR and the
stall fan-out (4-6 LUT levels plus high-fanout routing). The same redirect
also drives the regfile read address (rs1_addr/rs2_addr come from the masked
instruction), the decoder and imm_gen, and flush_id resets every ID/EX flop
(~200 bits, mostly data fields that need no clearing). Fitness is roughly
Fmax / cycles, and none of this changes cycle count.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Make the redirect signal arrive only where it is functionally needed (the PC
mux select, the EX/MEM capture, and a small flush of ID/EX valid/control),
and remove it from everything else. No architectural behaviour changes and
the cycle count is unchanged; only the combinational dependency structure
changes.

1. if_stage.sv: the NOP mask and valid depend only on the `flush` input,
   not on `redirect`: `out.instr = flush ? NOP : imem_data;
   out.valid = !flush;`. On a redirect cycle the wrong-path instruction in
   ID is discarded anyway: flush_id=1 zeroes ID/EX unless dmem_stall holds
   ID/EX, and in the held case ID/EX does not capture. So the NOP mask is
   only needed for imem_stall, where a garbage instruction could otherwise
   reach dmem_wen (dmem_wen is not gated by valid).
2. hazard_unit.sv: `flush_if = imem_stall` (drop `|| redirect`). Add a
   comment that load_use_hazard and redirect are mutually exclusive
   because a LOAD in ID/EX cannot be a branch or jump. load_use, stall_if
   and stall_id then no longer depend on redirect. stall_if/stall_id/
   stall_ex_mem/hold_mem_wb keep their current definitions. flush_id =
   (load_use || redirect) && !dmem_stall is unchanged, so redirect is
   still late only on flush_id.
3. id_stage.sv: on flush (not reset), clear only `valid` and `ctrl` in
   ID/EX. The data fields (pc, rs1_val, rs2_val, imm, rd, rs1_addr,
   rs2_addr, instr) are left to the existing !stall capture, with no
   reset term, so flush_id drives about 25 flops instead of about 200. A
   bubble with ctrl=0 and valid=0 has no side effect: reg_write, mem_read,
   mem_write, is_branch, is_jump and div_op are all 0, so forwarding,
   load-use, redirect, dmem and the regfile ignore its stale data. Reset
   still clears the whole register. RVFI fields of valid=0 slots are
   don't-care, and the memory-side outputs are already gated by
   ren/wen.

   updates if needed.

worst path should be ID/EX -> forward mux -> compare -> redirect ->
PC-mux/flush, a few LUT levels shorter, giving Fmax a bump from about
45 MHz toward 50-55 MHz at identical cycle count. Verification is the
existing cocotb suite (test_pipeline covers branch/jump/load-use/dmem
stall flows), cosim and the riscv-formal checks.

title: Make redirect a leaf signal: raw-bit hazard check, no NOP forcing in IF, control-only ID/EX flush
motivation:
After the divider was moved out of EX (hyp-001: 45.2 MHz), the reported worst
path is regfile/ID-EX operand -> EX forward mux -> compare/adder -> redirect ->
u_if -> u_hazard -> u_id -> u_if (pc), 44 cells / 22 levels / 27 ns. The tail of
that path (u_ex -> u_if -> u_hazard -> u_id -> u_if) is not a real data
dependence: if_stage forces the fetched instruction to NOP when
`flush || redirect`, hazard_unit then computes load_use_hazard from the
NOP-forced rs1/rs2 bits (core.sv wires `if_id_w.instr[19:15]/[24:20]`), and
load_use feeds stall_if/stall_id/flush_id, which fan back into the PC mux and
the ID/EX register. Functionally, redirect already has priority over stall at
the PC (`else if (redirect) pc <= redirect_target`) and over everything at the
ID/EX register (flush_id = ... || redirect, sync-clears the register), so the
redirect -> NOP -> load_use -> stall -> pc/ID-EX loop is a structurally present
but semantically false path that STA still times. Prior iterations only
attacked arithmetic blocks (divider, multiplier) and a BTB that lengthened this
same cone; none restructured the control topology around redirect.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Restructure the pipeline control so that `redirect` (the late EX-computed
signal) is a leaf that only drives (a) the final PC next-state mux and (b) the
synchronous clear of the ID/EX control bits, and never re-enters the fetch/
decode/hazard cone.
(1) core.sv: feed hazard_unit.if_id_rs1/rs2 from the raw fetch word
    `io_imemData[19:15]` / `[24:20]` instead of the NOP-forced `if_id_w.instr`.
    A spurious load_use on a wrong-path/stalled-fetch instruction is harmless:
    redirect still wins at the PC and flush_id is already 1 under redirect; on
    an imem stall the PC already holds and ID/EX captures a bubble either way.
(2) if_stage.sv: stop forcing the instruction and valid on `redirect`.
    Emit `instr = imem_stall ? NOP : imem_data` and `valid = !imem_stall`
    (flush_if reduced to the imem_stall term). On redirect the ID/EX register
    is cleared by flush_id (or held under dmem_stall, exactly as today), so the
    wrong-path word never reaches EX. Make the PC next-state an explicit
    priority mux  pc_d = redirect ? redirect_target : (stall ? pc : pc+4).
(3) id_stage.sv: narrow the ID/EX flush so redirect/load-use clear only the
    side-effecting bits (valid, ctrl.reg_write, mem_read, mem_write, is_branch,
    is_jump, is_illegal) instead of sync-resetting all ~170 payload flops; the
    data fields (pc, rs1_val, rs2_val, imm, rd, rs addrs, instr) are only
    reset by `reset`, and only load when !stall. This cuts redirect/flush_id
    fan-out from ~170 flops to ~8, which shortens the routed delay of the
    critical net. A bubble keeps valid=0 and all side-effect bits 0, so the
    forward unit (keys off ctrl.reg_write), div_op (requires in.valid) and
    load_use (keys off ctrl.mem_read) see a true NOP.
(4) hazard_unit.sv: drop flush_if's redirect term (now only imem_stall) and keep
    flush_id/stall_id as is. No architectural behaviour changes: retirement
    order, RVFI trap, memory traffic and cycle counts for CoreMark should be
    identical to hyp-001 (same taken-branch penalty of 1 bubble, same load-use
    stall), so iterations/cycle is unchanged and the gain is pure Fmax: removing
    ~4-5 LUT levels (NOP mux, load_use compare, stall OR, ID/EX enable) from the
    27 ns cone should move Fmax from ~45 MHz toward ~52-57 MHz. Remaining
    critical path becomes the true forward -> compare/adder -> redirect -> PC
    cone, which can then be attacked directly in later iterations.

title: Zero-bubble decode-in-fetch predictor: JAL always + 128-entry agree-BHT branches, direction-only EX recovery
motivation:
Every taken branch / JAL / JALR resolves in EX and costs exactly 1 bubble (the one wrong-path
fetch behind it). The prior BTB study (hyp-20261002-003-r1s2, replayed over the real CoreMark
retirement trace) measured: 2,937,037 retired instructions, 4,514,348 cycles (CPI 1.54) under the
22% stall model; 532k conditional branches (296k taken), 49.6k JAL, 13.8k JALR -> 359k redirect
bubbles = 8.0% of all cycles. A BTB at fetch removed most of that (+7% modeled) but added a
30-bit EX-side pred_next compare and a BTB next-PC mux on the redirect -> PC cone, which after
the divider fix (hyp-001) is the Fmax-limiting path (27 ns regfile -> forward -> compare ->
redirect -> PC). That attempt also claimed a static decode-time scheme "cannot help because decode
already happens in the IF cycle" -- that reasoning is backwards: in this core the IF/ID bundle is
combinational (imem_data is consumed in the same cycle the PC presents the address, and in the
timed netlist imem_data comes straight from a flop), so the instruction word is already in hand
during the cycle it is fetched. A B-/J-type immediate adder on that word can therefore steer the
NEXT fetch with zero bubbles, with no BTB tags/targets at all (the target is recomputed from the
instruction, so there is no capacity limit and no stale-target problem), and EX validates only the
1-bit *direction*, which is cheaper on the critical redirect cone than a 30-bit target compare.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move taken-branch/JAL steering from EX into the fetch cycle and make EX a pure direction checker.

(1) if_stage.sv -- decode-in-fetch prediction. From the raw imem_data word compute
    is_jal = (opcode == 1101111); is_br = (opcode == 1100011) && funct3[2:1] != 2'b01
    (EXCLUDE reserved funct3 = 2,3 so it exactly matches decoder.sv's is_branch);
    imm_b / imm_j exactly as imm_gen.sv; imm[1] must be 0 (otherwise do not predict: the
    target would be misaligned and EX's existing trap path must see an unpredicted instruction).
    pred_target = pc + (is_jal ? imm_j : imm_b); pred_raw = ~imm[1] & (is_jal | (is_br & dir)).
    next_pc = pred_raw ? pred_target : pc + 4, then the existing priority
    `reset > redirect(EX) > !stall` is untouched: EX redirect is still the LAST mux level, so the
    critical redirect -> PC select path is not lengthened (pc+4 vs pred_target is resolved
    earlier from registered pc + flop-sourced imem_data). Stalls need no extra gating because every
    stall reason (load-use, imem, dmem, div) already holds the PC register, and the held
    instruction is simply re-fetched/re-predicted next cycle. Export `pred_taken` in the if_id_t
    bundle = pred_raw & ~(flush | redirect) so bubbles/NOPs/flushed fetches never carry a
    prediction (add `pred_taken` to if_id_t and id_ex_t in core_pkg.sv; id_stage.sv just latches it
    into ID/EX, which is already zeroed on flush/reset).

(2) Direction predictor: 128-entry direct-mapped table of 2-bit saturating counters indexed by
    pc[8:2], held in flops inside if_stage.sv (do NOT add a new rtl file -- keep it in if_stage so
    the file list/order is unchanged), reset to 2'b10. Use the "agree" encoding so cold entries
    and aliasing default to static backward-taken/forward-not-taken: bias = imm_b[31] (backward);
    dir = c[1] ? bias : ~bias. JAL ignores the table (always taken). Training is done from the
    REGISTERED EX/MEM stage, one cycle after resolution, so it adds nothing to the critical
    redirect cone: when ex_mem_w.valid && ex_mem_w.ctrl.is_branch, with agree =
    (ex_mem_w.branch_taken == ex_mem_w.bwd), update counter[ex_mem_w.pc[8:2]] <= agree ?
    min(c+1,3) : max(c-1,0). Add a 1-bit `bwd` (= id_ex.imm[31]) to ex_mem_t, filled in ex_stage.
    Add if_stage ports bht_upd_en / bht_upd_idx[6:0] / bht_upd_taken / bht_upd_bwd wired from
    ex_mem_w in core.sv. (A held EX/MEM register only occurs for a mem op, never a branch, and a
    double update would be harmless anyway.)

(3) ex_stage.sv -- direction-only recovery. Define actual_dir = (is_branch & branch_cond) |
    (is_jump & ~is_jalr) (JAL counts as taken) and
      redirect = (is_jalr | (actual_dir ^ in.pred_taken)) & ~misalign_fault
      redirect_target = is_jalr ? {jalr_sum[31:1],1'b0}
                      : in.pred_taken ? in.pc + 4      // predicted taken, was not taken
                      : in.pc + in.imm;                // predicted not-taken, was taken (branch or JAL)
    A correctly predicted JAL/branch never redirects; a mispredicted one pays the same 1-cycle
    bubble as today (flush_if/flush_id/stall logic in hazard_unit.sv is unchanged because it keys
    off `redirect`). Using the generic XOR also makes any unforeseen pred/decoder disagreement
    self-healing instead of silent. misalign_fault, ctrl_with_trap, the alu_result = pc+4 link
    value for JAL/JALR and the RVFI pc_next expression (branch_taken ? target : pc+4, jump ->
    jump_target) stay exactly as they are, so rvfi_pc_wdata, trap and order are unchanged and
    riscv-formal / cosim see the identical retirement stream.

Expected cycle effect from the trace statistics above: all 49.6k JAL are removed from the bubble
count and the 296k taken branches become mostly free (a bimodal/agree table on CoreMark runs at
~92-95% accuracy; the 128 entries cover the ~341 redirecting static sites' hot set, 93% of dynamic
redirects fall in the hottest 64). Remaining bubbles ~50k (mispredicts ~35-40k + 13.8k JALR) vs
359k now -> ~300k fewer cycles of 4.51M = ~6.5-7% fewer cycles. Cost: +256 FF (+ ~150-250
LUT4 read/update muxing), one 30-bit adder in IF fed from flops, +2 flops in ID/EX / EX/MEM.
Fmax risk is low: the new imem_data -> decode -> adder -> next_pc path is ~10-12 ns against the
~27 ns redirect cone, and the redirect cone itself loses the JAL terms (jump_target/misalign for
JAL no longer feed redirect) while gaining one XOR with a registered bit.

title: Shorten EX alu_result -> EX/MEM -> dmem-address cone: fold JAL/JALR PC+4 into ALU operands, share one multiplier
motivation:
After the divider and predictor fixes the worst path (~27 ns arrival, 15 cells, modules
u_id > u_ex > u_alu > u_ex) ends at the dmem BSRAM: Gowin absorbs the dmem read-address
register into the BSRAM, so the D input of EX/MEM.alu_result (forward mux -> alu_a/alu_b mux ->
ALU -> div_op mux -> is_jump PC+4 mux -> reset/stall/div_stall clear) is the timed endpoint.
Every level after the ALU's own case mux (div_op mux, is_jump mux, sync reset to '0) is pure
overhead on that cone, and alu.sv builds three separate 32x32 multipliers (ss/uu/su) whose
product muxes all feed the same final case.

extra levels. (1) JAL/JALR return address goes through the ALU: add a decoded ctrl bit so

title: Move operand forwarding from EX into ID: EX reads only ID/EX flops, bypass network feeds the ID/EX capture
motivation:
Every recent run reports the same worst path (15 cells, ~27 ns): ID/EX flop ->
forward_unit compare/priority -> 3:1 EX forward mux (32 bits x 2, high fanout
select) -> ALU adder + result case mux + jump/div mux -> dmem BRAM address
(the EX/MEM.alu_result register is absorbed into the BSRAM address input, so
the ALU result is effectively timed to the BRAM address pins). The branch
compare -> redirect -> PC cone starts from the exact same forward mux, and the
DSP multiplier path also starts there. Micro-opts that only pruned the tail of
the redirect cone (r2s0 / r2s1) got ~5% because the shared FRONT of every EX
cone (5-bit rd/rs compare, priority select, fan-out-32 mux select, 3:1 mux,
plus the wb mux feeding the MEM/WB forward input) was untouched. Cycle count is
already good (4.20 M cycles with the zero-bubble predictor), so the remaining
lever is shortening what all EX cones have in common, with zero IPC cost.

forward_unit compare/priority -> 3:1 EX forward mux (32 bits x 2, high fanout
select) -> ALU adder + result case mux + jump/div mux -> dmem BRAM address
(the EX/MEM.alu_result register is absorbed into the BSRAM address input, so

DSP multiplier path also starts there. Micro-opts that only pruned the tail of

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Restructure the bypass network so forwarding is resolved in ID instead of EX
(the classic "forward into the ID/EX capture" topology). The EX stage then
consumes in.rs1_val / in.rs2_val straight from the ID/EX flops: no
forward_unit compare, no select fan-out, no 3:1 mux in front of the ALU,
address adder, branch comparator or divider. Every EX cone loses ~4-5 LUT
levels at its front and gains at most one 2:1 mux level at the ALU-result ->
ID/EX-capture end.

For the instruction I in ID in cycle t, the operand is selected (priority
younger-first, x0 never forwarded) from:
  P1 = instruction currently in EX (ID/EX):  value = ex result =
       is_jump ? pc+4 : (div_op ? div_result : alu_out)   [the same value
       that EX already writes into EX/MEM.alu_result]. Enable =
       id_ex.valid-agnostic: in.ctrl.reg_write && !misalign_jump && in.rd!=0
       (use misalign_jump only, NOT the late misalign_branch/branch_taken
       term, so the select stays off the compare cone; branches never have
       reg_write=1). Load producers are NOT forwarded here: the existing
       load-use hazard (id_ex.mem_read && rd match) still bubbles the
       consumer one cycle, exactly as today.
  P2 = instruction currently in MEM (EX/MEM): value = mem_to_reg ? load_data
       (post shift/sext, from dmem_rdata) : alu_result, enable = the
       mem_stage ctrl_with_trap.reg_write (so a misaligned load/store trap
       that clears reg_write also suppresses the forward) && rd != 0. A
       dmem stall holds ID/EX (stall_id already includes dmem_stall), so the
       capture never samples a not-yet-delivered load word.
  P3 = instruction in WB: already covered by reg_file's write-first bypass.
  else the regfile read.
Because the captured value is final, ID/EX operands are stable while the
register is held (div_stall, dmem_stall). That makes the EX-side MEM/WB
forwarding (fwd_mem_wb, and the retained-data trick in hold_wb) dead, the
divider's operand latch protocol still works unchanged, and div_rs1_q /
div_rs2_q (RVFI-only, pruned from the timed netlist) can be replaced by
in.rs1_val / in.rs2_val.

forward_unit.sv is kept (test_pipeline.py lists it in its source list) but
repurposed as the ID-side select generator: it compares the RAW fetched rs1/
rs2 bits io_imemData[19:15]/[24:20] (not the redirect/flush NOP-masked
if_id_w.instr, so late `redirect` does not reach the selects; a stale select
on a flushed/invalid ID bubble is harmless because ID/EX is cleared on
redirect and a NOP/invalid instruction's operands are never observed) against
id_ex.rd / ex_mem.rd, and outputs one-hot p1_hit / p2_hit. The late data
inputs only enter the last mux level before the ID/EX flops.

No change to stall counts, hazard_unit load-use logic, branch predictor,
RVFI values (rs1_rdata/rs2_rdata are the same architecturally-forwarded
values, just captured one stage earlier) or the divider FSM, so
CoreMark cycles stay ~4.198 M and the gain is pure Fmax. Expected: the
15-cell ID/EX -> BRAM-address path drops by ~4-5 cells (~7-8 ns of the
~27 ns), redirect -> PC and DSP-multiplier cones lose the same front; the new
limiters (imem BRAM Dout -> raw rs compare -> bypass mux -> ID/EX, ALU result
-> bypass mux -> ID/EX, DSP mult) are all estimated at <= ~15-18 ns, so Fmax
should rise from ~46 MHz toward 55-60 MHz even with place-and-route noise.

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-002-r3s1 (improvement, +17.73%): Moving operand forwarding out of EX and into the ID/EX capture (EX reads only ID/EX flops; a one-hot P1=EX-result / P2=MEM-result bypass mux sits in front of the ID/EX flops, with selects compared on the raw `io_imemData` rs fields and the existing load-use bubble kept) reached 128.67 vs 109.29 at unchanged cycle count and beat the ~14% predicted, because it removed the shared front of every EX cone (rd/rs compare, fan-out-32 select, 3:1 mux) from the ALU->BRAM-address, branch->redirect->PC and DSP-multiplier paths at once, where the tail-only pruning in r2s0/r3s0 gave just ~5-8%; when a path family shares one front end, relocate that front end to the previous stage rather than trimming each tail, and keep new selects off late signals (`redirect`, branch-taken) so only data enters the last mux level.

title: Decoupled predicted-fetch skid buffer: BHT/JAL-steered PC keeps fetching during backend stalls
motivation:
The decode-in-fetch predictor (r2s2) already makes taken branches and JAL
zero-bubble; the remaining control loss is only ~1 bubble per mispredict or
JALR (r1s2's retirement-trace study: 13.8k JALR and ~500k cond. branches
in 2.94M instructions), so a better direction/target predictor alone is
capped at ~2-3% of cycles and cannot clear the 4.6% acceptance bar. The
big remaining loss is that the predictor-steered PC is lock-stepped to the
backend: any dmem stall, load-use bubble or divide holds the PC
(stall_if), so the ~78% imem-ready slots in those cycles are thrown away
and the same instruction is re-fetched later, while an independent ~22%
imem stall still costs a full bubble whenever it lands on a cycle the
backend could have consumed an instruction. The stall generator draws
imem_ready and dmem_ready from two independent xorshift draws, so the two
stall streams are uncorrelated and can be overlapped.
Calibration: 109.29 / 45.876 MHz = 2.38 CoreMark/MHz, i.e. ~420k
cycles/iter over ~294k instr/iter => CPI ~1.43. imem alone costs 1/0.781 = 1.28;
the rest is backend stall slots (dmem 22% x ~30% mem ops, load-use) at
s ~ 0.09 per cycle plus ~0.025 control bubbles. Markov model with
f=0.781, s=0.09: lock-stepped 0.711 instr/cycle (CPI 1.41 + 0.025 ~ 1.43,
matches the measured CPI); one-entry skid buffer 0.763 (CPI 1.31 + 0.025 =
1.336, ~+7% fewer cycles); two entries 0.775 (+8.7%); infinite buffer is
capped at f = 0.781. One entry therefore captures ~80% of the achievable
gain for ~66 flops and one 2:1 mux.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Decouple the predicted fetch stream from the ID consumer with a one-entry
skid buffer plus zero-latency bypass, kept inside if_stage.sv (the BHT,
JAL/branch steering, pred_target adder, EX direction check and the BHT
training path are unchanged; EX redirect stays the last next-PC mux level).

if_stage new state: buf_valid, buf_pc[31:0], buf_instr[31:0], buf_pred.
New if_stage input: `stall_id` (the existing hazard_unit stall_id =
dmem_stall | load_use | div_stall, i.e. "ID/EX will not capture the head
this cycle"); imem_ready is now consumed inside if_stage.

  head_valid = buf_valid | imem_ready
  head_instr = buf_valid ? buf_instr : imem_data
  head_pc    = buf_valid ? buf_pc    : pc
  head_pred  = buf_valid ? buf_pred  : pred_raw
  out.instr  = (redirect | !head_valid) ? NOP : head_instr
  out.valid  = head_valid & !redirect
  out.pred_taken = head_pred & out.valid
  accept     = imem_ready & !(buf_valid & stall_id)   // PC advances
  load_buf   = imem_ready &  (buf_valid ^ stall_id)  // fetched word -> buf
  pc <=  redirect ? redirect_target : accept ? next_pc : pc
  buf_valid <= redirect ? 0 : load_buf ? 1 : (buf_valid & stall_id)
  buf_{pc,instr,pred} <= {pc, imem_data, pred_raw} when load_buf
next_pc / pred_raw / BHT lookup still use the raw fetch at `pc`, so the
prediction is made once at fetch and rides in the buffer; a bypassed
instruction (buffer empty, no stall) has exactly today's latency, so there
is no extra mispredict/JALR bubble. During a dmem stall, load-use bubble
or divide the PC fetches one instruction ahead into the buffer; a later
imem stall is then covered by the buffered instruction.

hazard_unit: stall_id/flush_id/stall_ex_mem/hold_mem_wb unchanged;
stall_if (PC-hold) and the imem_stall term in flush_if are retired because
if_stage derives accept/head_valid itself (a spurious load_use from garbage
imem_data while !head_valid is harmless: ID/EX gets a bubble either way and
accept is already 0 because imem_ready=0). The load-use compare must read
the head instruction's rs1/rs2 (buf_instr or imem_data, selected by the
buf_valid flop) instead of raw io_imemData, and must NOT use the
redirect-gated out.instr (keeps redirect off the stall cone, per r2s2).
core.sv only rewires these ports.

Why it should hold Fmax: the worst path is the EX forward->ALU->EX/MEM cone
(27 ns); the front end gains one flop-selected 2:1 mux on the ID side
(imem_data is an LFSR flop in the timed netlist, buf_valid is a flop) and
the PC-enable cone has the same kinds of inputs as today's stall_if
(imem_ready flop, dmem_stall, load_use, div_stall) with redirect still
last. Retirement order, pc_wdata and rvfi fields come from EX/MEM/WB as
before, so formal contracts (order, pc continuity, trap) are unchanged;
liveness holds because the buffer only fills when the backend stalls and
drains on backend progress or redirect flush.
Verify with test_pipeline.py (drive imemReady/dmemReady with a random
pattern in a new cocotb test; zero-wait cycle-count asserts for load-use
and divide spacing may need updating since the PC now runs ahead) and the
CoreMark cosim with --istall --dstall (CRCs must still match).

title: Take late EX redirect off the regfile-read/decode cone: IF->ID NOP mask on imem stall only, x0 check out of regfile read

The r3s1 champion (128.67, 54.0 MHz) reports its worst path as
ID/EX.rs2_val flop -> cpu/u_ex -> cpu/u_id -> cpu/u_if -> cpu/u_rf ->
cpu/u_id -> ID/EX.rs1_val flop (45 cells, 23.4 ns). That route is
branch compare -> `redirect` -> if_stage's `out.instr = (flush||redirect) ?
NOP : imem_data` -> id_stage rs1_addr/rs2_addr -> 32:1 regfile read mux
(+ x0 / write-first compare) -> ID-side bypass mux -> ID/EX capture.
Forwarding moved into ID turned the late EX `redirect` into the head of a
second long cone: it now gates the *address* of the regfile read even though
the result is discarded on redirect (flush_id zeroes ID/EX on redirect, and
a dmem stall holds ID/EX so nothing is captured). Earlier redirect-pruning
attempts (r2s0/r2s1) only trimmed tails of a different cone; here the
redirect-gated NOP mask is literally the reported critical path, so removing
it should pay more than the ~5% they saw.

title: Register the branch/JALR redirect: resolve in EX, redirect from EX/MEM flops (MEM-stage redirect)
motivation:
After r3s1 moved forwarding into ID, the worst path (23.4 ns, 45 cells) is
ID/EX.rs2_val -> EX compare -> redirect -> if_stage NOP mask on
io_imemData -> regfile read address -> 32:1 read mux -> bypass mux ->
ID/EX.rs1_val. The late EX `redirect` is still the root of several cones:
the PC next-mux, flush_id (ID/EX clear), the IF NOP mask (which also gates
the regfile read addresses), and div/stall interactions. Prior micro-opts
(r2s0/r2s1) only pruned a few leaves of that cone and got 5-8%; the lesson
from r3s1 is that relocating a shared front end beats trimming tails.
The 32-bit compare / misalign check is the shared front end of every
redirect consumer, so move the redirect *consumers* one stage later.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Keep branch/JALR resolution (compare, jalr_sum, direction check, misalign
trap) in EX exactly as today, but do not fan the result out combinationally.
Capture a 1-bit `redir` (is_jalr || (actual_dir ^ pred_taken)) &&
!misalign_fault into the EX/MEM register; the redirect target is the
already-captured EX/MEM.pc_next (jump_target / branch_target / pc+4 -
these are exactly the three redirect targets). `redirect` and
`redirect_target` become flop outputs of EX/MEM (u_ex.out.redir /
out.pc_next), so the PC next-mux, flush_id, the IF NOP mask, load-use gate
and everything else downstream of `redirect` start from flops instead of
from the compare. Compare->redirect becomes compare->1 flop.
Squash semantics (the branch is now in MEM when the redirect fires, so TWO
wrong-path instructions are in flight: the one in EX and the one in comb
ID/IF): when `redirect` is asserted (a) PC <= EX/MEM.pc_next (redirect keeps
top priority over stall in if_stage), (b) ID/EX is flushed to '0 (existing
flush_id path), (c) the instruction currently in EX is converted to a
bubble at the EX/MEM capture (reg_q <= '0, same as the div_stall bubble

!redirect, otherwise a wrong-path DIV would start the FSM and a later
correct-path DIV would wait on the wrong `done`). A branch in MEM is never
a memory op, so dmem_stall is 0 while redirect is asserted (no hold/redirect
conflict). Because the squashed EX instruction never reaches MEM, no
wrong-path load/store can touch dmem and no wrong-path rd can be forwarded
(ID is flushed in the same cycle). Wrong-path ex_res forwarded into the ID
capture is discarded by the flush.

are roughly 2-3% of instructions, so ~+2% cycles. Benefit: the redirect
cone (compare -> misalign -> redirect -> PC mux / flush / NOP mask ->
regfile read -> bypass -> ID/EX) disappears from the top of the timing
report; the remaining long cones are ALU -> ex_res -> bypass and
dmem_rdata -> align -> bypass, which are shorter. The regfile read
addresses in id_stage are also taken from the raw io_imemData rs fields
(valid because ID/EX is flushed on redirect), removing the second path from
`redirect` into the regfile mux even if a flop-derived redirect were
slower than expected. Expect Fmax +10-15% for ~2% cycle loss.

title: Two-entry decoupled fetch queue behind the predictor-steered PC, with redirect-free regfile/hazard addressing
motivation:
Direction/target prediction is essentially exhausted: the decode-in-fetch
predictor (r2s2) makes JAL and taken branches zero-bubble, a mispredict or
JALR costs exactly one bubble (IF+ID share a cycle, resolve in EX), and the
retirement-trace numbers (~500k cond. branches, 13.8k JALR in 2.94M instr)
cap any better BHT / RAS / gshare at ~1-1.5% of cycles - below the 4.6%
acceptance bar. The real front-end loss is that the predictor-steered PC is
lock-stepped to the backend: every dmem stall, load-use bubble or divide
holds the PC (stall_if), so the ~78% of those cycles in which imem_ready=1
are thrown away and the word is re-fetched later, while the independent ~22%
imem stalls still cost a full bubble. Measured CPI is 4.198M cycles / ~2.94M
instr = 1.43; imem alone costs 1/0.781 = 1.28, so a perfectly decoupled
front end is bounded by ~1.30 (~9-10% fewer cycles). The one-entry skid
buffer of r3s2 (rejected only because r3s1 merged first and the Fmax delta
was P&R noise, 45.159 vs 45.876 MHz) measured 4,019,055 vs 4,197,768 cycles
= -4.3%, about 0.55x of a Bernoulli stall-model estimate (the model gives
+8.1% for 1 entry, +10.3% for 2, +11.1% for 3, +11.4% for 4). The second
entry is the cheap step that moves the cycle gain from ~4.4% to ~5.5-6%,
i.e. over the acceptance bar by itself. The current worst path (23.4 ns,
45 cells) is ex compare -> redirect -> if_stage NOP mask -> regfile read
address -> read mux -> ID bypass mux -> ID/EX.rs1_val, so the same edit
that adds the queue head mux should take the regfile read address off the
late `redirect` signal.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the lock-stepped PC/ID coupling in if_stage with a 2-entry fetch
queue (e0 = oldest, e1) and a flop-selected head bypass, keeping the existing
decode-in-fetch predictor (JAL always, 128-entry agree-BHT, EX 1-bit
direction check, JALR unpredicted) bit-for-bit.

Fetch side. The PC register is the *fetch* PC and now runs ahead of ID.
Each cycle the fresh word {pc, imem_data, pred_raw} is formed exactly as
today and is valid iff imem_ready. Queue entries store {pc[31:2], instr,
pred_taken} (65 flops each) plus valid bits v0/v1. Head selection:
head = v0 ? e0 : fresh; head_present = v0 | imem_ready. The head mux select
is a flop (v0), so it adds only one 2:1 LUT level in front of decode, and
nothing redirect-dependent.

Handshake (no redirect): ID consumes the head when !stall_id (stall_id =
dmem_stall | load_use | div_stall, unchanged). pop = v0 & !stall_id.
accept = imem_ready & !(v1 & stall_id) (queue not full after the pop);
PC <= next_pc iff accept. A fresh word that is accepted is stored iff
(v0 | stall_id) (otherwise it is bypassed straight into ID), written to e0 if
the queue is empty after the pop, else to e1; on pop e1 shifts into e0.

Add a 2-entry queue {pc[31:2], instr, pred_taken} with valid bits v0/v1 (cleared on reset and redirect). head = v0 ? e0 : {pc, imem_data, pred_raw}; head_present = v0 | imem_ready. pop = v0 & !stall_id; accept = imem_ready & !(v1 & stall_id); PC enable = redirect | accept (redirect still the last mux level); store fresh iff accept & (v0 | stall_id) into e0 (queue empty after pop) or e1, e1 shifts into e0 on pop. out.pc = head.pc, out.instr = (redirect | flush | !head_present) ? title: Dedicated load/store address adder into the dmem BRAM address and late (MEM-forwarded) multiplier off the ex_res cone
motivation:
The worst path after r4s2 (18.98 ns, 9 cells, 73.07 MHz) is ID/EX flop -> ALU -> ex_res -> dmem BSRAM
(endpoint dmem_2_dmem_2_0_0_s). The dmem is an async-read array addressed by io_dmemAddr = EX/MEM.alu_result,
so Gowin absorbs that address register into the BSRAM and the BRAM read-address pin is fed by the D input of
EX/MEM.alu_result, i.e. ex_res = is_jump ? pc+4 : (div_op ? div_result : alu_out). That cone contains the whole
ALU case mux (adder, shifters, logic, SLT, three 32x32 multipliers on DSP) plus the jump/divider muxes, although a
load/store address is just rs1 + imm. The same ex_res cone also feeds the P1 bypass mux in ID, so the DSP
multiplier (about 8 ns of combinational delay on GW2A) sits in front of both the BRAM address and the bypass.
Prior rounds showed that when several path families share one front end, moving that front end out beats
trimming each tail (r3s1, r4s2), and that multiplies are rare in CoreMark (matrix only, ~2% of instructions),
so one extra bubble for a dependent multiply consumer is cheap.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Two coupled edits on the EX result cone, cycle-neutral except for a multiply-use bubble:
(1) Dedicated address generator. ex_stage computes maddr = in.rs1_val + in.imm with its own 32-bit adder (loads
and stores always use rs1 + imm, is_auipc = 0) and registers it in a new ex_mem_t field `maddr` (same hold /
div-bubble handling as the other EX/MEM fields). mem_stage drives io_dmemAddr from in.maddr and uses
in.maddr[1:0] for byte_mask, misalign, load-shift and aligned_addr instead of in.alu_result. The BRAM read address
is then a bare flop-to-adder-to-BRAM path with no op mux, no div mux and no is_jump mux, and no multiplier.
(2) Late multiplier. MUL/MULH/MULHSU/MULHU results (and their RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS stand-ins) come out of alu.sv on
a separate `mul_out` port (alu `out` is 0 for those ops) and are merged only at the EX/MEM.alu_result flop:
`reg_q.alu_result <= is_mul ? mul_out : ex_res`. ex_res (the P1 bypass source) no longer contains the multiplier.
A new decoder-set ctrl bit `late_res = mem_read | is_mul` (registered in ID/EX, 1 flop) replaces
id_ex.ctrl.mem_read in hazard_unit's load-use term, so a consumer of a multiply in EX gets the same one-cycle
bubble as a load consumer and then picks the product up through the existing P2 (MEM, mem_res) bypass. The
ex_res_en/p1_hit logic is unchanged: a spurious P1 hit on a late op is discarded by the flush_id bubble exactly
as it is for loads today.
Optional tidy that rides along: replace the three 64-bit product expressions in alu.sv by one shared signed
33x33 multiplier (operand sign-extension bits = signed_a & a[31], signed_b & b[31]) so one DSP macro and one
fan-out of rs1/rs2 serves MUL/MULH/MULHSU/MULHU (r3s0 already showed this maps cleanly and cycle-neutral).
The divider path, branch/redirect logic, fetch queue and BHT are untouched. Expected effect: the BRAM-address
endpoint drops from ~19 ns to roughly adder + BRAM setup (~9-10 ns); ex_res -> bypass mux -> ID/EX loses the DSP
term; the new critical path moves to the redirect cone or the regfile/forward cone (~15-16 ns), giving about
+8-12% Fmax against ~1-2% extra cycles from multiply-use bubbles.

title: Registered two-cycle multiplier unit: take the DSP array out of the EX result / dmem-address cone
motivation:
Gowin's report for the current champion (183.49, 73.05 MHz) shows the
worst path is NOT redirect/forwarding any more. Path 1 (18.98 ns, 9 cells,
and paths 2-5 are the same cone) is:
  ID/EX.pc_9 -> alu_a operand mux (1.9 ns incl. route)
    -> cpu/u_ex/u_alu/mul_uu DSP (1.3 ns route + 3.76 ns inside the DSP)
    -> five LUT levels of the ALU result / div / jump mux chain (~5 ns)
    -> EX/MEM.alu_result hold mux -> dmem BSRAM address pin (+0.95 ns route).
The BSRAM address register is absorbed from EX/MEM.alu_result, so the
timed endpoint is the combinational EX result. The combinational 32x32
multiplier (mul_ss / mul_uu / mul_su, 6 DSPs) alone contributes ~5.1 ns
of the 13.65 ns net data path (~37%) and sits in front of every consumer
of alu_result (ex_res bypass into ID/EX, EX/MEM.alu_result, BSRAM
address), yet it is used by only a few percent of retired instructions
(the matrix kernels of CoreMark). The divider was the same story in the
first iteration (a rare, deep op that dominated the cone; moving it to a
multi-cycle unit gave the biggest single Fmax jump). r1s1 tried the same
for the multiplier when the critical path was still the redirect cone and
lost; with redirect/regfile/forward cones now fixed, the DSP is the
actual longest pole, so the lesson applies now.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the combinational multiplier inside alu.sv with a registered
multi-cycle multiplier that follows the divider's protocol. New
rtl/multiplier.sv takes the held ID/EX operands (rs1_val / rs2_val taken
directly from the flops, bypassing the alu_a/alu_b operand muxes) and
computes ONE shared 33x33 signed product with the signedness flags decoded
from alu_op (MUL/MULH: both signed; MULHSU: rs1 signed; MULHU: unsigned) -
one multiplier instead of three, which also frees ~4 DSPs. The product word
is selected (MUL -> [31:0], MULH* -> [63:32]) and captured in a 32-bit
`mul_q` register at the end of the first EX cycle, so the timed path is
ID/EX flops -> DSP -> 2:1 select -> mul_q (~9.5 ns net vs 13.65), with no
ALU result mux behind it. ex_stage treats MUL* like the divider: in the
first cycle (mul_op && !mul_done_q) it asserts the existing div_stall
output (renamed ex_wait or OR-ed in; hazard_unit already holds ID/EX / PC
/ fetch queue on it and EX/MEM captures a bubble), sets mul_done_q; in the
second cycle alu_result = mul_q and the instruction moves on, clearing
mul_done_q unless a dmem stall holds EX/MEM (mul_done_q next =
mul_op && (!mul_done_q || stall), mul_q is only rewritten while
!mul_done_q so it is stable under a dmem stall). A MUL is never a branch,
load or jump, so no redirect / load-use interaction arises while it
waits, exactly as for the divider. alu_result becomes
`alu_out | ({32{mul_op}} & mul_q) | ({32{div_op}} & div_result)` - alu.sv
returns 0 for MUL*/DIV* in the non-ALTOPS branch, so the late-arriving
ALU adder/shifter output sees only one OR level (replaces the current
div_op ? : mux and the DSP mux inputs). Under RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS nothing
changes: alu.sv keeps its xor stand-ins and mul_op is tied to 0 (like
div_op), so formal is unaffected and the real branch is covered by
test_multiplier.py (new, exact bit vectors for MUL/MULH/MULHSU/MULHU
incl. 0, -1, INT_MIN, and the held-operand / dmem-stall-in-second-cycle
behavior) plus cosim against the Python ISS. The `test_alu.py` MUL*
vectors that run in the real (non-ALTOPS) build must move to the new
multiplier test since alu.sv no longer produces MUL results there.
Cost: one extra EX cycle per MUL/MULH* (about 2-3% of CoreMark retired
instructions, i.e. roughly -2.5% iterations/cycle); +32 FF, -4 DSP. Gain:
with the DSP removed from the cone, the remaining worst paths are the
ALU adder -> result mux -> BSRAM / bypass and the compare -> redirect
cones, estimated at ~10.5-11 ns net (~90-95 MHz), i.e. +20-25% Fmax,
netting about +15-20% fitness. If the next limiter turns out to be the
BSRAM-address cone through the ALU result mux, a follow-up can give the
memory address its own rs1+imm adder; this hypothesis deliberately does
not bundle that.

title: Fetch-stage return-address stack: predict JALR returns, validate against the next-in-order PC
motivation:
After the decode-in-fetch predictor (JAL always, 128-entry agree-BHT) and the 2-entry
fetch queue, the only control-flow class still unpredicted is JALR: it always
redirects from EX, flushing the head instruction and the fetched word and restarting
fetch (~1 cycle + the 22% imem-stall chance on the restart fetch, ~1.3 cycles).
I measured the CoreMark 2K -O3 binary on the Python ISS (2.94M instructions):
532k conditional branches (18%), 9.3% mispredicted by the current 128-entry
agree-BHT (49.4k), 49.6k JAL (all predicted), 13.8k JALR of which 13,772 are
`ret` (jalr x0,0(ra)) matched by 13,772 `jal ra` calls, and 0 indirect calls. A
4-entry RAS mispredicts only 12 of the 13,772 returns on this trace. So control-flow
redirects are ~2% of the ~4.2M cycles in total; returns are ~0.4-0.6% of them and
are the only redirect class that can be removed completely (direction mispredicts
are data-dependent: 256-1024-entry bimodal only reaches 7.5%, and gshare with 2-8
history bits is worse, 7.7-9.9%, so a wider/history BHT is not worth a longer
pc -> BHT-read -> next_pc cone). This hypothesis is therefore a low-risk,
small-gain predictor change that does not touch the ALU -> ex_res -> ID bypass
critical path; it is deliberately honest that the predictor category's ceiling on
this core is ~2% of cycles.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a small circular return-address stack (4 entries x 30 bits, 2-bit top pointer,
no overflow/underflow tracking - wrap just mispredicts, EX still validates) to
if_stage, updated speculatively from the instruction word already in hand in the
fetch cycle (same decode-in-fetch idea as JAL/BHT):
  - push pc[31:2]+1 when an accepted word is a call: JAL or JALR with rd == x1;
  - a "ret" = JALR, funct3=0, rd == x0, rs1 == x1, imm12 == 0 (imem_data[31:20]==0)
    is predicted taken with target = RAS top and pops the pointer. imm == 0 is
    required so the EX check needs no adder. Non-ret JALRs stay unpredicted.
The RAS read is a flop-sourced 4:1 mux, parallel to the existing B/J imm adder, so
pred_target gains one 2:1 select (is_ret ? ras_top : pc+imm) and pred_raw gains an
OR of is_ret; the EX redirect stays the last next-PC mux level. The RAS update is
gated only by `accept` (no `redirect` gating, to keep the late redirect off the ~120
enables); wrong-path pollution after a mispredict only costs accuracy, never
correctness.
Validation needs no extra storage in the fetch queue / ID/EX: when a JALR with
pred_taken is in EX, the predicted next PC is exactly the PC of the head of the
fetch queue (if_id_w.pc = v0 ? e0.pc : fresh.pc, where fresh.pc is the fetch PC),
because the head is always the next in-order instruction behind the one in EX. EX
therefore does one 32-bit equality `rs1_val == {if_id_w.pc[31:2], 2'b00}` (both
flop-sourced, no adder, cheaper than the branch magnitude compare it sits next to).
Wire if_id_w.pc into ex_stage as a new input. New EX redirect terms:

title: Take EX redirect off the ID/EX capture cone: drop the if_stage NOP mask and narrow the ID/EX flush to valid+ctrl
motivation:
The r5s0 champion's reported worst path (17.9 ns, 38 cells, 13 logic levels) is
ID/EX.rs2_val -> EX branch compare -> `redirect` -> if_stage `emit` NOP mask on
out.instr (modules listed: u_ex, u_if, u_id/u_imm) -> imm_gen opcode/immediate
mux -> ID/EX.imm flop. After the dedicated load/store address adder and the late
multiplier merge removed the ALU/DSP -> BSRAM-address cone, the late compare ->
redirect signal fanning into the *data* capture of ID/EX is the new longest
pole. That fanout is also redundant: hazard_unit already clears ID/EX with
flush_id = (load_use | redirect) & !dmem_stall, and under dmem_stall ID/EX holds
(stall_id) so it never captures the masked word; divide-in-EX never coexists with
a redirect. So the `flush | redirect` term in if_stage's emit mask (which gates
out.instr, out.valid and out.pred_taken ahead of decoder + imm_gen + the ID/EX D
inputs) adds 1-2 LUT levels and a ~230-flop fanout net behind `redirect` for no
functional purpose. Additionally flush_id currently drives the synchronous
reset of every ID/EX flop (pc, rs1_val, rs2_val, imm, instr, ...), i.e. a
~230-load net behind the latest signal in the design, although only the
side-effect bits of a bubble (valid, pred_taken, ctrl) need to be zero.
r2s0 tried a version of this before the fetch queue and the P1/P2 bypass move
existed and measured about half the modelled gain; the cone is now the explicit
limiter, so the same edit is aimed at the right endpoint this time.

Remove `redirect` (and the flush_if/flush input) from if_stage's output mask so
out = head_present ? head : NOP/valid=0 depends only on flop-selected signals
(v0, imem_ready), and shrink the ID/EX register's flush/reset domain to only
valid, pred_taken and the whole ctrl_t bundle (~25 flops). All data fields
(pc, rs1_val, rs2_val, imm, rd, rs1_addr, rs2_addr, instr) get a plain
`else if (!stall)` capture with no reset or flush (they are unobservable while

valid, mem/branch/jump/div decode need ctrl or valid; pred_taken is cleared so
a bubble cannot raise `redirect`). `redirect` then reaches only the PC mux
(already its last level), the fetch-queue valid bits, and a ~25-flop
synchronous clear, instead of the decoder/imm_gen/bypass-adjacent D cones and a
230-flop reset net. The change is cycle-neutral (same bubbles, same stalls,
same redirect penalty) so the gain is pure Fmax. Expected Fmax gain is bounded
by the gap to the next-longest cone (dmem address path ~ 15-16 ns), so I size it

realise at roughly the gap to the next path).

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-001-r6s0 (regression, +1.55%): Taking `redirect` out of if_stage's NOP mask (out = head_present ? head : NOP) and narrowing the ID/EX flush/reset to valid+pred_taken+ctrl (data fields captured with plain `if (!stall)`) was cycle-neutral but reached only 216.17 vs r5s0's 212.88, about a quarter of the ~6% predicted and under the ~4.6% merge margin, which is the second time (after r2s0's half-size gain) that trimming `redirect`'s sinks has underdelivered because the late rs2_val -> branch compare -> `redirect` -> PC-mux/flush cone is untouched and the endpoint just moves to the next-longest path (dmem address ~15-16 ns); stop proposing redirect-fanout pruning on its own and either shorten the compare->redirect cone itself (r4s1's registered redirect is the lever that paid) or bundle the pruning with a change that does.

title: Registered EX redirect (MEM-stage redirect) on top of the fetch-queue / maddr tree
motivation:
The r5s0 critical path (17.9 ns arrival, 38 cells, 13 levels) is
ID/EX.rs2_val -> u_ex branch compare -> redirect -> if_stage emit mask
(instr NOP-gate) -> imm_gen -> ID/EX.imm. The late EX `redirect` is the
root of every remaining long cone: the PC next-mux, the fetch-queue valid
bits, flush_id (clears all ID/EX flops, high fanout), the if_stage NOP
mask feeding decoder / imm_gen, and the div/stall gating. r5s0 just removed
the ALU -> BSRAM-address cone that used to hide this one, so the redirect
cone is the limiter again (and the r5s0 lesson says to re-read it next).
r4s1 already proved the fix: registering the redirect (compare -> 1 flop)
took Fmax up ~4x the modelled gain on the pre-fetch-queue tree for ~2%
cycles, passed formal + cosim, and lost its round only because the
fetch-queue change (which independently removed redirect from the
regfile-address cone) merged first. That change was never re-applied on
top of the current tree. The 2-entry fetch queue now makes it simpler:
regfile/hazard/forward compares already read the unmasked head, so the
only consumers left are the PC mux, queue valid bits, flush_id, the emit
mask and the divider start gate.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Keep branch/JALR resolution (compare, jalr_sum, actual_dir ^ pred_taken,
misalign check) in EX exactly as today, but capture only a 1-bit
`redir = (is_jalr || (actual_dir ^ pred_taken)) && !misalign_fault`
into the EX/MEM register, and drive the global `redirect` /
`redirect_target` from the EX/MEM flops: redirect = ex_mem.redir,
redirect_target = ex_mem.pc_next (pc_next already equals the correct
recovery address in every redir case: JALR sum, pc+imm for a taken branch
or JAL that was not predicted, pc+4 for a predicted-taken branch that fell
through; misaligned targets never set redir and pc_next reverts to pc+4).
Compare -> redirect -> {PC mux, v0/v1 queue clear, flush_id, emit mask,
div gate} becomes compare -> 1 flop, and all of those consumers start from
a flop. The if_stage -> decoder / imm_gen -> ID/EX cone loses the whole
32-bit compare in front of it.

Squash semantics (the branch B is in MEM when redirect fires, so the
instruction B+1 in EX and B+2 in comb ID are wrong-path):
  (a) PC <= EX/MEM.pc_next and the fetch queue is emptied (existing
      `redirect` priority in if_stage: reset > redirect > accept);
  (b) ID/EX is flushed to '0 through the existing flush_id =
      (load_use || redirect) && !dmem_stall (B in MEM is never a memory op,
      so dmem_stall = 0 whenever redirect = 1; no hold/redirect conflict);
  (c) the instruction in EX (B+1) is turned into a bubble at the EX/MEM
      capture: add `redirect` as an input of ex_stage and clear reg_q to
      '0 (same branch as the div_stall bubble) when it is asserted, so no
      wrong-path load/store reaches dmem, no wrong-path instruction retires
      or trains the BHT, and redir itself is 0 in the bubble;
  (d) gate div_op with !redirect (and therefore div_stall) so a squashed
      wrong-path DIV/REM never starts the divider FSM (a later correct-path
      divide would otherwise wait on the wrong `done`).
Wrong-path ex_res / mem_res forwarded into the ID/EX capture in this cycle
is discarded by the flush. BHT training already comes from the registered
EX/MEM stage and is unchanged. rvfi_order / pc_wdata are unaffected (the
squashed instructions never retire, pc_next of B is unchanged).

Cost: redirect penalty 2 -> 3 bubble cycles, redirects are only ~2-3% of
instructions with JAL steering + the agree-BHT, so ~+2-3% cycles. Benefit:
the compare/redirect cone leaves the top of the timing report; the next
limiters are the ALU -> ex_res -> P1 bypass -> ID/EX.rs*_val cone and the
multiplier -> EX/MEM.alu_result cone, both estimated ~1.5-2.5 ns shorter
than the current 17.9 ns-arrival path, so Fmax should rise ~10-15% for a
net ~+7-10% fitness. Formal needs the usual check (liveness / pc_fwd /
unique / ill): a squashed instruction must never assert rvfi_valid, and
redirect must be a pure function of EX/MEM flops.

title: Registered mispredict recovery for the BHT/JAL predictor: capture the 1-bit direction check in EX/MEM and redirect fetch from the flop
motivation:
The r5s0 champion (212.88, 84.89 MHz) reports its worst path as
ID/EX.rs2_val -> EX compare (eq/lt/ltu, branch_op mux) -> actual_dir ^ pred_taken -> `redirect`
-> if_stage NOP mask (emit = head_present & ~(flush | redirect)) -> imm_gen/decoder -> ID/EX.imm
(17.9 ns arrival, 13 logic levels, modules u_ex > u_if > u_id/u_imm). The same late `redirect`
also drives the PC next-mux, v0/v1 clear, flush_id (sync clear of ~170 ID/EX flops) and the
div_op/EX-hold interplay. Every previous fix removed a different cone from the top of the
report (divider r1, forwarding-to-ID r3s1, fetch queue r4s2, dedicated address adder r5s0) and
each exposed the redirect cone again. r4s1 (registered redirect) was the biggest single
Fmax gain measured on the pre-fetch-queue tree (128.67 -> 173.20, ~4x its prediction) and was
only ranked a regression because r4s2 merged first in the same round; its remaining limiter
then was the ALU -> BSRAM-address cone, which r5s0 has since removed. The decode-in-fetch
predictor (JAL always taken, 128-entry agree-BHT with BTFN fallback) already keeps redirects
to ~2% of cycles (49k BHT mispredicts + 13.8k JALR out of ~4.0M cycles), so the recovery path
can afford one more cycle of latency: the predictor's job is to make the mispredict rare,
which is exactly what makes a slow (registered) recovery cheap.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Keep prediction exactly as it is (fetch-stage JAL + agree-BHT steering, EX validating only the
1-bit direction), but make mispredict RECOVERY a registered event. In EX compute
redir = (is_jalr || (actual_dir ^ pred_taken)) && !misalign_fault as today, but capture it only
into a new 1-bit ex_mem_t.redir flop (alongside the already-registered pc_next, which is
exactly the corrected next PC for all three redirect cases: branch_target when a
predicted-not-taken branch was taken, pc+4 when predicted-taken was not taken, jump_target for
JALR; misaligned cases already fall back to pc+4 and never set redir). The top level then drives
`redirect` = ex_mem_w.redir and `redirect_target` = ex_mem_w.pc_next from flops, so the PC
mux, fetch-queue v0/v1 clear, if_stage NOP mask, flush_id and load-use gating all start at a
flop instead of the compare: compare -> 1 flop.
Squash rules (the mispredicted branch is now in MEM when recovery fires, so the wrong-path
instruction already in EX plus the one in ID/IF must die):
  (a) PC <= EX/MEM.pc_next, fetch queue emptied (existing redirect priority in if_stage:
      reset > redirect > accept);
  (b) ID/EX is cleared (existing flush_id = (load_use | redirect) & !dmem_stall, now flop-driven);
  (c) the instruction currently in EX is turned into a bubble at the EX/MEM capture: in
      ex_stage the `div_stall` bubble branch becomes `else if (div_stall || redirect) reg_q <= '0`
      (so no wrong-path load/store ever reaches dmem, no wrong-path RVFI retirement, and the
      wrong-path instruction cannot set a new redir);
  (d) div_op is gated with !redirect so a squashed DIV/REM never starts the divider FSM
      (div_stall must be 0 whenever redirect is 1);
  (e) a branch in EX/MEM is never a memory op, so dmem_stall (stall_ex_mem) is 0 while redirect
      is 1 and the EX/MEM hold never conflicts with the redirect; BHT training from EX/MEM is
      unchanged. Wrong-path ex_res forwarded into the ID capture in the redirect cycle is
      discarded by the same flush_id.
Cost: mispredict / JALR penalty goes 2 -> 3 cycles, about +1.5-2% cycles on CoreMark
(~63k redirects of ~4.0M cycles, one cycle each, plus imem-stall interaction on the restart
fetch). Benefit: the compare -> redirect -> {PC mux, imm/decoder NOP mask, ID/EX clear, queue
valid bits} cone leaves the timing report; the next-longest cones are ALU -> ex_res -> ID bypass
mux -> ID/EX.rs*_val and dmem_rdata -> align -> mem_res bypass, both shorter than the current
17.9 ns worst path (r4s1's registered-redirect tree already topped out on the since-removed
ALU -> BSRAM-address cone). Expect Fmax +15-20% for ~2% fewer iterations/cycle, net roughly

implementation_notes:
# Implementation notes — registered mispredict recovery (hyp-20261002-003-r6s2)

## What changed

Prediction is untouched (fetch-stage JAL + 128-entry agree-BHT, EX validates the
1-bit direction). Only the *recovery* became a registered event:

- `core_pkg.sv`: `ex_mem_t` gains `logic redir;` (registered mispredict / JALR
  recovery flag). `branch_target` was dropped from `ex_mem_t` (nothing read it).
- `ex_stage.sv`:
  - The combinational `redirect` / `redirect_target` outputs are gone.
    `redir_nxt = (is_jalr || (actual_dir ^ pred_taken)) && !misalign_fault` is
    captured only into `reg_q.redir`.
  - `redirect` is now an **input** (= EX/MEM.redir, a flop output). The EX/MEM
    capture branch is `else if (div_stall || redirect) reg_q <= '0`, so the
    wrong-path instruction in EX when recovery fires becomes a bubble
    (no dmem access, no RVFI retirement, cannot set a new `redir`).
  - `div_op` is gated with `!redirect` so a squashed DIV/REM never starts the
    divider (and `div_stall` is 0 whenever `redirect` is 1).
  - `ex_res` / `ex_res_en`, the dedicated `maddr` adder and the late multiplier
    merge are untouched.
- `core.sv`: `redirect = ex_mem_w.redir`, `redirect_target = ex_mem_w.pc_next`
  (continuous assigns from the EX/MEM flops); `redirect` is fed to if_stage,
  hazard_unit and back into ex_stage. BHT-update wiring unchanged.
- `hazard_unit.sv`, `if_stage.sv`, `mem_stage.sv`: comment-only updates
  (no functional change; `flush_if = redirect`, `flush_id = (load_use | redirect) & !dmem_stall`
  now start at a flop).
- `test/test_pipeline.py`: gap expectations for a mispredicted branch updated
  2 -> 3 cycles (`backward_branch_loop_predicted`, `forward_branch_trains_to_taken`);
  new cases `recovery_squashes_wrong_path_store`, `recovery_squashes_wrong_path_div`,
  `recovery_back_to_back_mispredicts`, `recovery_squashes_wrong_path_jalr`,
  `recovery_squashes_wrong_path_branch_behind_jalr` (wrong-path SW/DIV/LW/JALR/branch
  never retire, never write dmem or a register, pc_wdata -> next pc_rdata chain and
  rvfi_order stay consistent, recovery is exactly 3 cycles).

## Why it is correct (timeline)

B = mispredicted branch/JALR. Cycle t: B in EX, `redir_nxt` captured at the end
of t. Cycle t+1: B in MEM, `redirect = 1`:
PC <= EX/MEM.pc_next, fetch queue emptied, IF NOP mask on, ID/EX cleared
(`flush_id`), and the wrong-path instruction in EX is squashed to a bubble at the
EX/MEM capture. Cycle t+2: the corrected target is fetched. Penalty 2 -> 3 cycles.

- `pc_next` already is the corrected PC in all three cases (JALR: jump_target;
  predicted-not-taken branch that was taken: branch_target; predicted-taken
  branch that was not taken: pc+4); misaligned cases fall back to pc+4 and never
  set `redir`. rvfi `pc_wdata` chain therefore unchanged.
- `dmem_stall` is 0 while `redirect` is 1 (the branch in MEM is not a memory op),
  so the EX/MEM `stall` hold never competes with the squash; `flush_id` is not
  masked by `!dmem_stall` in that cycle.
- `div_stall` is 0 while `redirect` is 1 (div_op gated), and the divider is
  IDLE then (a DIV ahead of B has left EX; a DIV behind B first reaches EX in
  the recovery cycle, where it is gated).
- A dmem stall *before* B resolves just holds B in EX (EX/MEM and ID/EX both
  hold), so `redir` is captured when the stall ends; no early/duplicate redirect.
- BHT training still comes from EX/MEM (`valid & is_branch`); squashed wrong-path
  branches are bubbles there so they never train.
- The old load-use comment ("on redirect EX holds a branch/jump") no longer holds
  (EX holds a wrong-path instruction), but a spurious load-use stall in the
  recovery cycle is harmless: `flush_id` has priority over `stall` in id_stage and
  the fetch queue is cleared by `redirect` (reset > redirect > accept for the PC).

## Deviations from the hypothesis text

None functionally. `branch_target` removed from `ex_mem_t`; `if_stage` left
as-is apart from comments (its `flush | redirect` mask is now two copies of the
same flop signal; synthesis merges them).

## Concerns

- Expected cost ~+1.5-2% cycles (one extra cycle on ~63k redirects of ~4.0M).
- `redirect_target = EX/MEM.pc_next` is a high-fanout flop (also feeds MEM/WB
  pc_next); the compare -> pc_next mux -> flop path in EX is now the compare's
  endpoint instead of the PC/IF/ID cone.

## Status

- `verilator --lint-only -Wall -Wno-MULTITOP`: clean.
- cocotb `test_pipeline.py`: 23/23 pass (incl. the new recovery tests and the
  3-cycle gap checks).
- Local formal / cosim / timing: see the final section appended below.

### Local results (final)

- Formal (`RTL_DIR=cores/bench/rtl CORE_NAME=bench bash formal/run_all.sh`, nret=1
  wrapper auto-selected): **53 passed, 0 failed** on the first attempt.
- Cosim (`NRET=1 make cosim TARGET=bench`): **passed** (selftest + CoreMark, 2 ELFs).
  Note: the plain `make cosim TARGET=bench` builds with the default NRET=2 and
  fails to compile main.cpp against this nret=1 core; that is a local invocation
  detail, not an RTL issue.
- `make timing TARGET=bench` (Gowin, place option 0): **96.45 MHz** (vs 84.89 for
  r5s0), worst path now ID/EX rs*_val -> ALU (u_ex/u_alu) -> EX/MEM.alu_result /
  ID bypass (15.66 ns, 7-10 cells); the compare -> redirect cone is gone from the
  top of the report. Expected cycle cost ~+1.5-2%.

title: Flatten the 12.5 ns cone wall: pre-muxed ALU B operand, AUIPC on the PC adder, raw-operand multiplier with pre-decoded selects, registered redirect
motivation:
`make timing` on the r5s0 champion (place_option 0) shows the top 25 setup paths are a flat wall at
12.1-12.6 ns data delay, not one dominant cone: (a) ID/EX.rs2_val -> branch compare -> `redirect` ->
if_stage emit mask -> imm_gen -> ID/EX.imm (38 cells), (b) ID/EX.ctrl.is_auipc / pc_N -> alu_a mux -> ALU
-> ex_res -> P1 bypass -> ID/EX.rs1_val/rs2_val (10 cells), (c) the same front mux -> ALU ->
EX/MEM.alu_result. Prior single-cone fixes each moved only 1.5-3.5% (r6s0 emit-mask pruning, r6s1/r6s2
registered redirect: 220.43 = +3.55%, under the 4.6% margin) because the placer simply re-equalises
to the next cone in the wall. After the redirect was registered, the report's worst path became
rs2_val[31] -> EX/MEM.alu_result[0] in 7 cells inside u_alu (the multiplier family, 15.66 arrival), with
the ALU front-mux cones right behind it. So a gain above the margin needs the three EX-side cones cut
together, each by roughly one LUT level / one high-fanout net. All three edits are small and local.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Four small edits that shorten every cone in the wall by about one LUT level, ~64 extra flops, no new
stalls, the only cycle cost is the 2->3 bubble redirect penalty (~1.6% cycles, measured in r6s1/r6s2):
(1) AUIPC off the ALU: alu_a becomes plain rs1 (no `is_auipc ? pc : rs1` mux, which puts a fanout-32
flop net and a LUT in front of the adder). AUIPC's result pc+imm is already computed by EX's
`in.pc + in.imm` adder (branch_target); fold it into the existing JAL-side mux: ex_res =
(is_jump | is_auipc) ? (is_jump ? pc+4 : pc+imm) : alu_result, where the pc-side mux is off the ALU path
(flops -> adder -> mux in parallel with the ALU).
(2) Pre-muxed B operand: ID/EX gets a new 32-bit field `alu_b` = alu_src ? imm : bypassed-rs2, built in
id_stage as the final AND-OR of the existing one-hot P1/P2/regfile bypass legs plus an imm leg (p1/p2
hits qualified by !alu_src, using the decoder's alu_src), so ex_res stays in the last LUT level.
rs2_val is kept unchanged for stores, the branch compare, EX/MEM write_data and RVFI. EX's ALU then
reads rs1_val and alu_b straight from flops: no alu_src mux/fanout-32 net in front of the carry chain.
(3) Multiplier off the ALU muxes and the alu_op compares: the DSP reads raw rs1_val / rs2_val (MUL* always
have alu_src = is_auipc = 0); the sign-extension bits come from pre-decoded ctrl flops (mul_sgn_a =
MULH|MULHSU, mul_sgn_b = MULH, set by the decoder); the result is merged with one pre-decoded one-hot
AND-OR at the EX/MEM.alu_result D input (mul_lo ? p[31:0] : mul_hi ? p[63:32] : ex_res) instead of
the lo/hi alu_op compare followed by an `is_mul` compare. ALTOPS stand-ins stay on `mul_out`.
(4) Registered redirect exactly as in r6s2 (hyp-20261002-003-r6s2 implementation_notes in
experiments/log.jsonl, formal + cosim passed there): resolve compare/jalr_sum/misalign in EX, capture a
1-bit `redir` in EX/MEM, drive redirect/redirect_target from EX/MEM.redir / EX/MEM.pc_next, squash the EX
instruction to a bubble and gate div_op with !redirect. This removes the compare -> PC-mux / fetch-queue
valid / flush_id / emit-mask cone (a), and with `redirect` a flop output the emit-mask and ID/EX flush
in id_stage/if_stage are free to keep as they are.
Expected: cone (a) disappears, (b)/(c)/(multiplier) each lose ~0.7-1 ns, so the median Fmax should land
near 96-100 MHz (vs 84.89) for ~1.6% more cycles, i.e. roughly +7-10% fitness. If only the registered
redirect landed it would still reproduce the +3.55% already seen, so the downside is bounded.
