lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-001-r7s0 (improvement, +9.15%): Cutting every cone of the flat ~12.5 ns post-r5s0 timing wall in one change (AUIPC pc+imm moved off the ALU onto EX's existing PC adder, a pre-muxed `alu_b = alu_src ? imm : rs2` ID/EX field so the adder has no operand mux or fanout-32 select in front, the DSP reading raw rs1/rs2 with decoder-computed `mul_sgn_a/b` and one-hot `mul_lo/mul_hi` selects merged at the EX/MEM.alu_result D input, plus the registered redirect) reached 232.36 vs 212.88 (above the ~7% predicted and clear of the ~4.6% margin), where the same registered redirect alone gave only +3.55% (r6s1) and redirect-pruning alone +1.55% (r6s0), because when the placer re-equalises to the next-longest path each single-cone fix is capped at the gap to its neighbour; when `make timing` shows a flat wall of near-equal endpoints, bundle one-LUT-level cuts to all the families together (move operand muxes and opcode compares into the previous stage's flops/decoder as pre-decoded ctrl bits) rather than proposing them one per slot, and re-read the new wall afterwards.

title: Registered MEM-stage redirect plus MEM-completed split multiplier (two coupled cone removals)
motivation:
Two single-cone fixes have each stalled just under the 4.6% merge margin because the
next limiter sits only a little behind. r6s1 (registered EX redirect, 1-bit redir in
EX/MEM, target = EX/MEM.pc_next) took the champion's 38-cell rs2_val -> branch compare
-> redirect -> PC/flush cone off the critical path and reached 220.43 (+3.55%, 89.3 MHz),
but its new worst path is rs2_val -> alu -> 33x33 DSP product -> EX/MEM.alu_result
(15.66 ns, 7 cells). r5s1 tried a 2-cycle EX multiplier on its own and lost because the
redirect cone was still the limiter. The two fixes are coupled: the redirect cone is the
limiter now (17.9 ns arrival) and the multiplier is the one right behind it (15.7 ns), so
only the pair moves Fmax by a margin worth merging.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
(1) Registered redirect (re-apply r6s1 on the fetch-queue / maddr tree). EX still resolves
branch_cond / jalr_sum / misalign, but captures only a 1-bit `redir` into EX/MEM
(redir = (is_jalr | actual_dir ^ pred_taken) & !misalign_fault & valid). The PC mux,
fetch-queue valid clear, IF NOP mask, hazard flush_id and BHT-independent paths are driven
from the EX/MEM flop with redirect_target = EX/MEM.pc_next (already the correct resolved
next PC in every redirect case). The instruction in EX in the redirect cycle is squashed at
the EX/MEM capture (bubble) and div_op is gated with !redir. Redirect penalty goes from 2
to 3 bubbles; predictor-steered JAL / BHT keeps redirects at ~2-3% of instructions so this
costs ~1.5% cycles.

(2) Split the multiplier across EX and MEM so no single cone contains the whole DSP array.
alu.sv builds four <=18x18 partial products from 16-bit halves of the (sign-extended)
operands: p_ll = al*bl (unsigned), p_lh = al*bh, p_hl = ah*bl, p_hh = ah*bh (ah/bh are
17-bit signed with sgn_a/sgn_b extension) and exports them, rather than the summed product.
EX/MEM registers the partial products (~4 x 34 flops, spare FF budget: 1956 of ~15k used)
directly at the DSP outputs, so the EX cone is flop -> operand mux/sign -> single 18x18
DSP -> flop (~1 DSP level, no fabric adder tree). mem_stage sums them
(p_ll + ((p_lh + p_hl) << 16) + (p_hh << 32), low or high 32 bits per MUL vs MULH*) into
MEM/WB.alu_result; that carry-chain sum is a short flop -> adder -> flop cone and is NOT
on mem_res (P2 bypass). Because the product only exists in MEM/WB, MUL* is treated as
"very late": a MUL in MEM cannot be bypassed (mem_res_en excludes it), so hazard_unit
stalls a consumer in ID while the producer is in EX (existing late_res) or in MEM with
the new mul flag (ctrl bit or an EX/MEM `is_mul` bit); once the MUL is in WB the
consumer reads it through reg_file's existing write-first bypass. That costs one extra
bubble per dependent MUL consumer (~1-1.5% cycles, MUL* is ~2% of CoreMark).
Under RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS keep the xor/add stand-ins on the existing alu_result path and
keep the same extra-stall rule so formal sees the identical pipeline timing; the real
DSP partial-product path stays under `ifndef`.

Expected: both ~15-18 ns cones leave the critical list, the new worst path is the
ALU -> ex_res -> P1 bypass -> ID/EX or dmem-address cone at ~12-13 ns, so Fmax 85 -> ~96-100
MHz at ~+2.5-3% cycles. Net ~+8% over 212.88. If the next limiter turns out to be within
~1 ns of the multiplier path the gain collapses to the r6s1 figure, so the implementer
should read the post-change critical path with `make timing` before tuning further.

title: Registered mispredict recovery with fetch-at-target: imem_addr muxed from EX/MEM flops so the corrected fetch starts the cycle after the redir flop, keeping the champion's 1-bubble penalty
motivation:
The champion's (r5s0, 84.89 MHz) critical path is rs2_val -> branch compare -> `redirect`
-> PC mux / queue clear / NOP mask / ID flush (38 logic cells). Registering the mispredict
(r6s1 / r6s2: 1-bit `redir` flop in EX/MEM, recovery from the flop in MEM) shrank the worst path
to 7 cells and lifted Fmax 84.89 -> 89.28 MHz (+5.2%), but cycles rose 3,987,604 -> 4,050,390
(+1.57%) because the corrected fetch now starts a cycle later (redirect penalty 2 -> 3 cycles,
2 wrong-path words fetched instead of 1). Net +3.55%, under the 4.6% merge margin, which is
why both r6s1 and r6s2 were ranked regressions.
The extra bubble is not intrinsic to registering the redirect. imem in the cosim and in the
timed netlist is a combinational function of `io_imemAddr`, and `io_imemAddr` is observed only
by the LED XOR, so the fetch address can be `redir ? EX/MEM.pc_next : pc`. That is a mux of
flops only, with no compare in front of it. The target word is then fetched in the same cycle
the `redir` flop is high, exactly the cycle the unregistered design fetched it. Registered
recovery then costs ~0 cycles and keeps the full +5.2% Fmax, i.e. fitness ~ +5% against the
champion. The pure-predictor cycle ceiling is tiny here: only about 49k mispredicts at ~2 cycles
each (~3% of cycles) are left, and the RAS in r5s2 gained 0.09%. The recovery path is the part
of the predictor that still has headroom.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Start from the r6s2 tree (champion + registered recovery) and add fetch-at-target.
Prediction itself (JAL always taken, 128-entry agree-BHT, decode-in-fetch) is unchanged.

1. EX/MEM captures a 1-bit `redir` (= (is_jalr || (actual_dir ^ pred_taken)) && !misalign_fault)
   and the resolved `pc_next` (already stored). core.sv drives `redirect = ex_mem_w.redir` and
   `redirect_target = ex_mem_w.pc_next`, both flop outputs. ex_stage takes `redirect` as an
   input. The wrong-path instruction in EX in the redirect cycle is squashed at the EX/MEM
   capture (`else if (div_stall || redirect) reg_q <= '0`), `div_op` is gated with
   `!redirect`, and `ex_res_en` is gated with `!redirect` so the P1 bypass cannot hand the
   squashed instruction's result to the target word entering ID.

2. if_stage: define `fpc = redirect ? redirect_target : pc`.
   - `imem_addr = fpc`.
   - `fresh.pc = fpc[31:2]`.
   - BHT read index = fpc[8:2].
   - `pred_target = fpc + imm_sel` and the fall-through is `fpc + 4`.
   To keep the mux out of the carry chain, compute the pc-based and the target-based
   adders / increments / BHT-counter reads in parallel and select with the `redirect` flop
   in the last level. This costs ~100-150 LUT4, against 4.2k used and a 10k budget.
   - While `redirect` is high the whole fetch queue is wrong-path, so treat it as empty:
     `head = (v0 & ~redirect) ? e0 : fresh`, `head_present = (v0 & ~redirect) | imem_ready`,
     and drop `flush`/`redirect` from the `emit` mask (the queue-ignore replaces it).
     The valid bits keep clearing on `redirect` as today.
   - PC update: `if (redirect) pc <= accept ? next_pc : redirect_target;
     else if (accept) pc <= next_pc`. An imem stall in the redirect cycle must still move
     PC to the target.
   - With `redirect` high, `stall_id` is 0, so the target word is consumed straight from the
     fresh port and never needs queue storage.

3. hazard_unit: `flush_if` and `flush_id` no longer include `redirect`; the NOP-masked or
   valid head from if_stage already produces the right ID/EX contents.
   `flush_id = load_use_hazard & !dmem_stall`. Gate the load-use term with `!redirect`
   (`id_ex_late_res & ~redirect`) so a wrong-path load/mul in EX does not stall the target
   word. dmem_stall is already 0 in the redirect cycle (MEM holds a branch/JALR), and
   `div_stall` is 0 via the `div_op` gate.

4. Cycle accounting: B in EX at t, `redir` high at t+1, target fetched and in ID at t+1, in
   EX at t+2. That is the same gap as the champion's combinational redirect (1 bubble).
   Wrong-path words fetched are X1 only, as before. Existing mispredict-gap assertions in
   test_pipeline.py stay as they are; they should not move from 2 to 3.

Expected: Fmax ~ 89 MHz as measured for r6s1/r6s2. The 7-cell ALU/multiplier -> alu_result
path becomes the limiter, and the compare -> PC / flush cone is gone. Cycles ~ champion
(+-0.3%). Fitness ~ 212.9 -> ~224 (+5%).
Risk: the redirect flop now fans out to the fpc mux, v0 gating, emit and squash logic, and
the fetch-address adders gain a parallel copy. If the IF cone shows up near the limit, fall
back to the slightly slower variant that keeps `head = v0 ? e0 : fresh` and masks `emit`
with `~(redirect & v0)`, storing the target word into the queue.

title: Shorten the ID front cone: write the regfile from MEM (no write-first/x0 on the read ports) and fold rd!=0 into decoded reg_write/late_res
motivation:
Cycles are at the imem floor (~4.05M cycles / 10 iters; IPC ~0.78 = the 22% imem stall rate with a 32-bit
fetch port), so fitness only moves with Fmax. After r7s0 cut the EX-side cones, the report's worst path
(place option 0, 16.78 ns, 8 cells) is the ID front cone: cpu/u_if/v0 -> head mux (v0 ? e0 : fresh) ->
head_rs1/rs2 -> reg_file read (rs==0 gate, write-first compare w_addr==rs, 32:1 mux) -> id_stage bypass
(P1/P2/regfile) -> ID/EX.rs2_val. Every level on that cone sits behind the high-fanout v0 select and the
address nets that fan out to ~256 mux inputs per port. Two of those levels are pure bookkeeping that can be
moved off the cone without any cycle cost: the regfile's own WB write-first bypass (compare w_addr against
the late head address + 2:1 mux + the x0 compare/mux) and the `rd != 0` 5-bit compares that sit in front of
the P1/P2 hit selects (ex_res_en / mem_res_en) and the load-use compare. r4s0 tried the x0 half in
isolation but was lumped with redirect pruning and died on a formal timeout, so this is a different, tighter
scope and it is bundled with the matching select-side trim (the r7s0 lesson: cut all families of the flat
wall by one LUT level together, since single cone fixes get absorbed by the next-longest path).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Three small, cycle-neutral edits that each remove roughly one LUT level from the regfile-read -> bypass ->
ID/EX cone and from the P1/P2 select cones that feed the same ID/EX D inputs.
(1) Regfile is written from the MEM stage instead of WB. The write port is driven by the MEM result that is
already the P2 bypass value: w_data = mem_res (load_data or alu_result), w_en = mem_res_en && ex_mem.valid &&
!stall_ex_mem (a dmem-stalled load in MEM does not write; it writes in the cycle the bus delivers, exactly one
write per instruction). An instruction that is in WB in cycle t has therefore already been written at the end
of cycle t-1, so the instruction in ID in cycle t reads it straight from the regfile: P3 coverage is preserved
with NO write-first compare/mux in reg_file. reg_file read ports become plain `regs[addr]` with x0 kept
constant zero (regs[0] is not a flop: `assign` it to 32'b0 and generate flops for 1..31 only, so no
`addr == 0` gate level and no reset-dependent x0 for formal). wb_stage/mem_wb remain only to feed RVFI
(rd_wdata keeps using the MEM/WB register mux), so retirement order/timing seen by riscv-formal and cosim is
unchanged. The extra load is only mem_res fan-out to the 31x32 D pins (enable decode is flop-sourced), which
is shallower than the existing mem_res -> 4-leg alu_b AND-OR leg.
(2) Fold `rd != 0` into the decoded control: in id_stage ctrl_decoded.reg_write = dec_reg_write &&
(in.instr[11:7] != 0) and late_res likewise (late_res only matters when a consumer can depend on rd). RVFI is
unchanged (rd_wen = reg_write && rd != 0 was already forced to 0 for x0), regfile write of x0 is already
impossible. Then ex_res_en = ctrl.reg_write && !misalign_jump, mem_res_en = ctrl_with_trap.reg_write, and
hazard_unit's load_use drops its `id_ex_rd != 0` term, so the P1/P2 hit selects (compare -> AND -> fan-out-32
select into the ID/EX rs1_val/rs2_val/alu_b AND-OR) lose a 5-input compare level.
(3) With P3 gone the ID bypass is exactly P1 / P2 / regfile, so keep it as the existing priority/one-hot
3-leg mux (rs1_val/rs2_val/alu_b) and make sure forward_unit's one-hot p2 exclusion term is only used by the
alu_b AND-OR (rs1_val/rs2_val keep the priority form), shaving the extra input off the rs1/rs2 select LUTs.
Expected: ~1 LUT level (~1-1.3 ns incl. routing) off the 16.8 ns front cone and ~0.5 ns off the P1/P2 select
cone, i.e. median Fmax ~99-101 MHz vs 94.1 at identical cycle count (~+5-7%). Risks: the load-data fan-out to
the regfile D pins could pull the BSRAM-output -> mem_res path up by a few tenths of ns, and the next-longest
EX cones (ALU -> ex_res -> P1, DSP -> EX/MEM.alu_result) may cap the gain; if mem_res fan-out is a problem the
implementer may instead register the write one stage later (keep WB write, but delete only the x0 gate and keep
(2)).

title: Registered IF/ID head: drop the v0-selected fetch bypass so regfile/bypass/load-use cones start at flops, with ID control pre-decoded in fetch
motivation:
The post-r7s0 worst path (arrival 16.78 ns, slack -6.49, 8 cells) is
cpu/u_if/v0 -> u_if (head = v0 ? e0 : fresh mux) -> u_rf (rs1/rs2 32:1
read mux + write-first bypass) -> u_id (P1/P2 bypass + alu_b AND-OR) ->
ID/EX.rs2_val. The start point is the high-fanout `v0` flop: it selects a
~63-bit head mux whose output (head_rs1/head_rs2) then fans out to the
regfile read muxes (32 bits x ~8 LUTs per address bit), the x0 / WB
write-first compares, the load-use compare and the four forward_unit
compares. The fetch-queue bypass ("fresh word straight to ID") is what
put that mux and its select in front of everything; it buys exactly one
cycle of latency after a redirect/empty queue and nothing in steady-state
throughput (the queue still accepts 0.78 words/cycle, and PC runs ahead of
ID either way). Redirects are only ~2-3% of CoreMark instructions
(r4s1/r6s1 lessons), so one extra bubble per redirect costs ~1.5-2% cycles,
whereas the regfile-address cone is the current Fmax limiter family.
Past single-cone fixes underdelivered (r6s0, r6s1) because the placer
re-equalises to the next-longest path, so this bundles the head-mux removal
with the other front-of-ID levels that become removable once the head is a
plain flop.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Make the fetch queue's ID-facing entry a true IF/ID register: ID always
reads e0 (valid = v0), never the fresh imem word. The fresh word is
always stored (into e0 if the queue is empty after the pop, else e1);
accept = imem_ready & ~(v1 & stall_id) is unchanged, store = accept,
occ/v0/v1 update unchanged except that `store` no longer excludes the
bypass case. Redirect still empties the queue (v0=v1=0) and PC <- redirect
target, so the first target instruction reaches ID one cycle later than
today (redirect penalty +1 cycle; predicted-taken JAL/BHT path is
untouched and still zero-bubble because next_pc is steered in the fetch
cycle from imem_data exactly as now).

Consequences for the timed cones:
 1. head_rs1/head_rs2 become e0.instr[19:15]/[24:20] straight from flops:
    the regfile read mux, write-first compare, x0 compare, load-use compare
    and forward_unit P1/P2 compares lose one LUT level (the v0 head mux) and
    the high-fanout v0 select net. Store 2-4 replicated copies of the
    5-bit rs1/rs2 fields in e0 (synthesis keep / separate regs) so each copy
    drives only 8-16 data bits of the regfile read tree and the compare
    logic gets its own private copy; the extra flops are cheap (FF 2020 of
    ~15k).
 2. Pre-decode in the fetch cycle (imem_data is already consumed
    combinationally there for the B/J predictor): decode `alu_src` and the
    imm_gen output once per fetched word and store them with the queue entry
    (e0/e1 gain alu_src + 32-bit imm, ~33 flops each; the full ctrl_t may be
    stored too if the implementer finds it cheap). The ID alu_b AND-OR
    selects (b_sel_ex/mem/rf = !alu_src & hit) then come from a flop, so the
    only late inputs to the ID/EX mux are the register-read data and the
    hit signals. imm_gen/decoder drop out of the ID-stage cone entirely.
 3. The flush/NOP-mask on the ID output (`emit ? e0.instr : NOP`) still
    depends on redirect, but only into ID/EX valid/ctrl, as today.

Nothing else in the pipeline changes: ex_stage, mem_stage, divider, alu,
hazard_unit (load-use is checked against e0 rs fields), forward_unit and
the registered redirect keep their current interfaces. The BHT, fetch
predictor, rvfi path and invariants are untouched. rvfi_order/valid are
driven from MEM/WB as before, so formal liveness/unique remain valid
(fewer stale-head corner cases than the bypass mux).

Budget: cycles +1.5-2% (one more bubble per ~2-3% redirecting instructions;
imem-stall bubble count unchanged since the queue still absorbs them).
Fmax: removes the v0-mux level (~1 ns) and the v0 fanout from the
8-cell regfile cone plus the alu_src/imm decode from the ID bypass cone,
worth ~6-9% on that endpoint; the next-longest paths (EX ALU->alu_result
~15.7 ns in r6s1 data, dmem address) cap the realised gain, hence the

title: Predictor-indexed branch-target instruction buffer: replay taken-branch targets from flops so imem stalls are hidden
motivation:
Cycle gains from direction prediction are exhausted (RAS gave +0.09%, bigger BHT / gshare
is capped at ~1% because mispredicts are only ~2-3% of instructions). What remains on the
front end is the instruction-supply ceiling: io_imemReady is low ~22% of cycles regardless
of address, so fetch delivers at most ~0.78 words/cycle and CoreMark runs at ~405k cycles
per iteration, within ~5% of that fetch floor. The predictor already knows, at the cycle a
predicted-taken branch/JAL is fetched, exactly which word will be fetched next (its
target). A tiny table keyed by the branch PC that remembers that target word lets the
next fetch be satisfied from flops instead of waiting on the random imem stall. Because
the table is read from the PC flop and replayed through flop-selected registers (same
style as the fetch queue's v0 select), it stays off the redirect, regfile-address and
ALU->bypass cones that set Fmax.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a 32-entry direct-mapped "branch-target instruction buffer" (BTIB) inside if_stage.sv,
indexed by pc[6:2] of a predicted-taken B/JAL and tagged with pc[31:7] (small LUT-RAM or
flops; async read from the pc flop). Each entry holds the first two instruction words at
the predicted target (K=2) plus a valid bit.

Replay: in a cycle where the fetched word is accepted and pred_raw=1 and the BTIB entry
for the current pc hits, capture {tgt_pc, w0, w1} into small replay flops (rp_v0/rp_v1,
rp_w0, rp_w1). Next cycle pc == tgt_pc (the registered redirect still has priority and
clears rp_v*), so the 'fresh' word is taken from rp_w0 with ready forced to 1 and the
following cycle from rp_w1 at tgt_pc+4. imem_ready is ignored during replay, so an imem
stall that would have hit the target fetch is hidden. 'fresh.instr' becomes
rp_v ? rp_w : imem_data and the ready term becomes imem_ready | rp_v, both selected from
flops (one extra LUT on the accept cone, not on imem_data->pred_target). The decode-in-fetch
predictor (JAL always, 128-entry agree BHT, 1-bit EX direction check) is applied unchanged
to the replayed word, so the BHT/EX recovery logic is untouched.

Training (no EX involvement, off every critical cone): remember the idx/tag of the last
accepted predicted-taken instruction in a flop; when the next accepted fetch word arrives
at its pred_target (from imem or a replay), write w0 into that entry, and the word after it
into w1 (valid bit per word). Instruction memory is static, so wrong-path training
is harmless; entries are cleared on reset. FENCE.I clears the BTIB valid bits.

The cycle model: taken branches/JALs are ~12% of fetches, the BTIB hits ~70-75%, and each
hidden fetch saves 0.22/0.78 = 0.28 cycles of exposed stall (two fetch slots per hit with
K=2), so ~3-5% fewer cycles for a small, flop-fed addition. Fmax is expected to be flat
because the new logic sits behind pc/BTIB flops and replay flops only. If the 4.6% margin
is not reached this is still the clearest way to move the fetch-bound floor, which pure
direction-prediction work cannot.

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-003-r8s2 (regression, -2.78%): A 32-entry fetch-side branch-target instruction buffer (BTIB: tag + two target words in LUT-RAM, rp_w0/rp_w1 replay flops forcing `rdy = imem_ready | rp_v0`, delayed training writes) landed at 225.90 vs r7s0's 232.36, below baseline against a ~4% prediction that was already under the ~4.6% merge margin, and the premise that it "stays off imem_data -> pred_target" did not hold because the replay mux `iw = rp_v0 ? rp_w0 : imem_data` replaced `imem_data` in every decode-in-fetch input (is_jal/is_br, imm_sel, the pred_target adder, the BHT bias) and in `fresh.instr`, so it adds a LUT level in front of the `v0 ? e0 : fresh` head mux -> regfile-read cone that is the current Fmax limiter (no Fmax/cycle split was recorded, so the cause is inferred); with cycles already within ~5% of the 0.78-word/cycle imem floor, any new source muxed into `fresh.instr` or the accept/ready term costs Fmax on the dominant cone for a cycle gain that cannot clear the margin, so hide imem stalls (if at all) behind the existing flop-selected queue entries rather than a second instruction source ahead of decode.

title: Pre-decode MEM load-align/store-lane controls in EX so BSRAM data -> mem_res -> bypass is a flat one-hot AND-OR
motivation:
After r8s0 (252.05, 102.09 MHz) the worst reported path is clock_ibuf > cpu/u_mem > cpu/u_id in 8 cells:
the dmem BSRAM output (dmem_rdata) -> mem_stage load extraction (rdata >> maddr[1:0]*8, byte/half pick,
sign bit mux4 fanned out to 24 bits, mem_sext/mem_width select, then `mem_to_reg ? load_data : alu_result`)
-> id_stage P2 bypass / alu_b AND-OR -> ID/EX D pins, and in parallel -> the 31x32 regfile D pins (r8s0
moved the regfile write to MEM, so mem_res now has fan-out ~34 per bit). Cycles are already at the imem
floor, so only Fmax matters. Everything mem_stage uses to steer that data (maddr[1:0], mem_width,
mem_sext, mem_to_reg, the misalign compare that gates mem_res_en) is a pure function of EX-stage values
that are available early in EX (the low two bits of rs1+imm are a 2-bit add, nowhere near the 32-bit carry
chain), so it can be decoded one stage earlier and registered instead of recomputed behind the BSRAM.

chain), so it can be decoded one stage earlier and registered instead of recomputed behind the BSRAM.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move all MEM-stage steering decode into EX and register it in EX/MEM, so the only logic between the BSRAM
output and the bypass is a flat AND-OR with flop-driven one-hot selects:
(1) EX computes a2 = (rs1 + imm)[1:0] with a dedicated 2-bit add (not the 32-bit maddr carry chain), the
misalign flag (word & a2 != 0, half & a2[0]) and registers new EX/MEM fields: ld_sel_b0..b3 (one-hot
"result byte0 takes rdata byte k": for byte loads k = a2, for half loads k = {a2[1],0}, for word loads
k = 0), ld_sel_h (result byte1 takes rdata byte {a2[1],1} for half / byte 1 for word, via per-byte one-hot),
ld_w_hi (bytes 2..3 take rdata bytes 2..3, word load only), a one-hot sign-source select sgn_k (which
rdata bit 8k+7 is the sign; all zero for unsigned loads and word loads, folded with mem_sext/width), and
sel_alu = !mem_to_reg. mem_to_reg is folded into all of these (they are all zero for non-loads), so
mem_res[i] = |(sel_k & rdata[..]) | (sel_alu & alu_result[i]) | sign, a flat AND-OR with no
`mem_to_reg ? load_data : alu_result` mux level after the sign/width muxes and no `>> (addr*8)`
barrel stage keyed off maddr.
(2) The misalign gating is folded at EX: EX/MEM.ctrl.reg_write/late_res are cleared for a misaligned
load (so mem_res_en = ctrl.reg_write straight from a flop with no maddr/mem_width compare in front of the
p2_hit select), is_illegal is set at EX (RVFI trap behaviour unchanged: the trap is still reported on the
same retirement), and EX/MEM also stores dmem_wen[3:0] and dmem_ren already gated by misalign and the byte
mask, plus the byte-replicated write data (wdata_rep) so the dmem write/enable output cones in u_mem are
just flop -> pin and the store byte-lane/replicate muxes leave u_mem.
(3) MEM/WB's RVFI-only fields (mem_addr, mem_rmask, mem_wmask, mem_wdata, read_data) are taken from the
registered fields (RVFI is pruned in the timed netlist, so only cosim/formal see them; retirement values
are bit-identical).
Cycle count is unchanged (no new stall, no extra bubble); cost is ~12 extra EX/MEM flops plus the 32-bit
wdata_rep register (replaces nothing; write_data stays for RVFI), and a few LUTs in EX where the short
2-bit-add cone has slack. Expected: the u_mem cone loses ~1 LUT level and the mem_res_en/p2 select cone
loses its misalign compare level, which should cut the ~16 ns BSRAM -> mem_res -> ID/EX path by 0.8-1.2 ns.
Because earlier lessons show single-cone fixes are absorbed by the next-longest path, the modelled gain is
only the gap to the neighbouring EX (ALU -> ex_res -> P1) cones.

title: Stall-filler I-cache: BSRAM direct-mapped word cache feeds only the fetch-queue entries when imem stalls
motivation:
Cycles sit at ~4.05M / 10 iterations, within a few percent of the fetch floor:
io_imemReady is low ~22% of cycles, so the single 32-bit imem port delivers at most
~0.78 words/cycle and the core runs at IPC ~0.74. All Fmax-side single-cone fixes
(r6s0, r6s1, r8s1) have been absorbed by the next-longest path, and the two attempts to
hide imem stalls from flops (RAS-style predictor r5s2, BTIB r8s2) either moved too few
fetch slots or put a new mux on `imem_data` in front of decode-in-fetch and lost Fmax.
The only structural way past the 0.78 words/cycle cap is to stop depending on imem for
words the core has already fetched: CoreMark runs the same ~6-8 KB of hot code 10 times,
so a plain direct-mapped word cache hits almost always. The lesson from r8s2 is where it
must NOT go: not into `imem_data` ahead of is_jal/is_br/imm_sel/pred_target, and not
into the `head = v0 ? e0 : fresh` bypass that feeds the regfile-address cone. This
proposal keeps both cones bit-for-bit as they are and uses the cache purely as a
second *fill source for the queue flops* during cycles where imem_ready = 0.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add rtl/icache.sv (instantiated from if_stage.sv): a 2048-word direct-mapped
instruction cache, index = pc[12:2], tag = pc[31:13], in BSRAM (data 2048x32 = 4 blocks;
sideband 2048x21 = {valid, is_ctrl, tag[18:0]}, 1-2 blocks; bsram was 4 of 46 so area is
fine). Synchronous read whose address is the D input of the existing `pc` flop
(reset / redirect / accept ? next_pc : pc, i.e. exactly the cone the pc flop already
has), so dout/tag are valid in the cycle where pc holds that address; both arrays are
written together in the same mode so a read-during-write returns a consistent pair.

Fill: every cycle in which a fresh imem word is accepted (imem_ready & accept) writes
{valid=1, is_ctrl = (opcode[6:2] is BRANCH or JAL), tag} and the raw word at index
pc[12:2]. The write data is straight from imem_data / pc flops (no decode of the cache
output is ever needed: is_ctrl is computed once at fill time on the already-existing
is_jal / is_br signals).

Use: `chit = en & valid_q & ~is_ctrl_q & (tag_q == pc[31:13])` (19-bit compare, ~2 LUT
levels after the BSRAM output; is_ctrl words are never served from the cache because a
taken B/JAL needs the decode-in-fetch next-PC steering, which stays on imem_data only).
`use_cache = ~imem_ready & chit`. Then in if_stage:
  accept = (imem_ready | use_cache) & ~(v1 & stall_id)
  store  = accept & (v0 | stall_id | ~imem_ready)   // a cache word is never bypassed
  fq entry D input: fresh_q = imem_ready ? {pc, imem_data, pred_raw} : {pc, cache_dout, 1'b0}
  next_pc = (pred_raw & imem_ready) ? pred_target : pc + 4
`head = v0 ? e0 : fresh` (the ID-facing / regfile-address / load-use / bypass-select
head) still uses only the imem `fresh` word, so the head mux, head_rs1/rs2 and the
redirect-priority structure are untouched; cache words only reach ID one cycle later
through the e0/e1 flops. The new logic sits only on (a) the pc-flop-D -> BSRAM address
pin (same cone as today's pc D input, plus BSRAM setup), (b) a ~3-level tag-hit ->
accept/store/v0/v1 enable cone fed from BSRAM outputs, and (c) a 2:1 mux on the
e0/e1 D inputs (not on `head`). Redirect still has top priority on pc and clears
v0/v1 exactly as now; wrong-path cache words are dropped with the queue.

Behaviour: after an ID stall (load-use, dmem, divide) or the first imem stall after a
redirect the queue holds one buffered word, and from then on an imem stall on any
hot, non-branch word is replaced by a cache fill into the queue (pop one, push one), so
the ID stage stops idling for ~77% of stall slots (~0.9 hit rate x ~0.85 non-control
words) instead of 100% of them; control words still wait for imem (decode-in-fetch
steering unchanged, JALR needs no steering). Since fetch and ID both run at 1
word/cycle the 2-entry queue is not overrun, and ID stalls simply back-pressure via the
unchanged `accept` ~(v1 & stall_id) term.

Cache initialisation without 2048 flops: an 11-bit sweep counter after reset writes
valid=0 to all indices (cache disabled, use_cache = 0, while sweeping, ~2048 cycles of
CoreMark startup, outside the start/stop MMIO markers; the BMC depth of riscv-formal is
far below 2048, so formal sees the original fetch behaviour and stays tractable).
Stores never modify code in CoreMark / selftest, so no invalidation path is added (if
the cosim selftest turns out to write code, add a per-store tag-invalidate from the
dmem write address instead of dropping the cache). rvfi / ordering / traps are
unaffected because only the source of already-accepted fetch words changes.
A cache-served word must be bit-identical to what imem would have delivered (static code
keyed by full pc[31:13] tag).

Expected: ~5-8% fewer cycles (ID idle slots from imem stalls fall from ~22% to a few %;
part of the stall slack was already overlapping with load-use/dmem/redirect bubbles, so
not the full 22%), with Fmax roughly flat because none of the current limiters
(BSRAM dmem -> align -> bypass, regfile read -> bypass, ALU/DSP -> ex_res) are touched
and the head-mux cone is unchanged. Main risk: the tag-hit -> accept cone after a
BSRAM output Tco becoming a new limiter; mitigation if so is to register `chit`
(use the cache word one cycle late, only when the queue already has an entry).

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-002-r9s1 (regression, +3.81%): A 2048-word direct-mapped stall-filler I-cache (BSRAM data + {valid,is_ctrl,tag} sideband read at the pc-flop D input, hit only for non-B/JAL words when `imem_ready = 0`, cached word pushed into the e0/e1 flops through a `fresh_q` mux and `next_pc` gated by `pred_raw & imem_ready`) reached 261.66 vs r8s0's 252.05, positive but under the ~6% predicted and the ~4.6% merge margin, while keeping the cache off `imem_data` and the `v0 ? e0 : fresh` head mux avoided the Fmax loss that put the r8s2 BTIB at -2.78% (no Fmax/cycle split was recorded, so both the split and the shortfall are inferred); a second fill source into the queue flops is a viable way past the 0.78-word/cycle imem cap, but it only converts stall slots where the queue already holds a word and the fetched word is non-control, and those slots overlap load-use/dmem/redirect bubbles, so budget it at roughly half the raw ~22% stall share (~3-4%) and expect it to clear the margin only when bundled with another change.

title: Single 16-entry loop trace buffer: BHT-detected loops replay into the fetch queue without imem handshakes
motivation:
Measured with the repo's Python ISS on the timed CoreMark region: 2,922,016 retired instructions
in 4,050,390 cycles (CPI 1.386). The imem stall floor alone is 1/0.78 = 1.282 CPI (3.75M cycles),
so the front end, not the predictor, is what bounds cycles. Mispredict recovery is only ~3.5% of
cycles in total (49k BHT mispredicts + 13.7k JALR, ~2.3 cycles each), which is why every
predictor-class cycle lever since r4s2 (RAS +0.09%, fetch-at-target -1.6%, bigger/better BHT)
stayed under the 4.6% merge margin. The only remaining way to cut the floor is to deliver
instructions without waiting on io_imemReady. r8s2's BTIB tried that for 2 words per taken
branch (-3.2% cycles) but lost ~12% Fmax because its replay mux sat in front of imem_data in the
decode-in-fetch cone and in front of the head -> regfile-read cone. A loop replay buffer that
only writes the existing queue entries e0/e1 leaves both cones untouched.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a loop trace buffer to if_stage.sv (no other module changes), serving the hot CoreMark inner
loops from flops/LUT-RAM instead of imem.

ISS model of exactly this policy on the CoreMark timed trace (record one iteration of a
backward-taken-branch loop with a dynamic path <=16 words and no JALR, then replay it until the
path diverges): ONE 16-entry trace serves 46.6% of all dynamic instructions (K=2/4/8 traces add
<1%, so a single buffer is enough; L=32 is no better than L=16). Replay exits (= redirects
that mostly coincide with loop-exit mispredicts the BHT also pays) are ~17.4k, ~0.6% of
instructions.

Mechanism:
1. Storage: tb[0:15] of {pc[31:2], instr, pred, last}, plain array with synchronous write and
   asynchronous read, no reset, so Gowin infers LUT-RAM (about 64 LUT4) rather than 1000 flops.
   Plus tb_valid, tb_pc0/tb_instr0/tb_pred0 flop copies of entry 0 (for the trigger compare),
   rec_on, rec_pc (30b), wp (4b), rep_active, rp (4b).
2. Record (only on `accept` of a live imem word, using the `fresh` fields): when not recording and not
   replaying, accept of a word with pred_raw && is_br && imem_data[31] (predicted-taken backward
   branch B) sets rec_on, rec_pc = pc, wp = 0, tb_valid = 0. While rec_on, each accepted word is
   written to tb[wp] with its pred_raw. If the word is JALR (opcode 1100111) or wp == 15, abort
   (rec_on = 0). If pc == rec_pc and pred_raw (the same back-edge again), mark that entry `last`, set tb_valid = 1, rec_on = 0;
   otherwise wp++. Any redirect aborts recording. Entry 0 is the loop head T (the word accepted
   right after B), so the trace is [T .. B].
3. Trigger: trig = accept & tb_valid & ~rep_active & (pc[31:2] == tb_pc0) &
   (imem_data == tb_instr0) & (pred_raw == tb_pred0). The full-word compare is required so
   replayed entries always follow the word actually fetched at T (formal pc_fwd / symbolic imem
   safety; EX only validates direction, never target, so a mismatching live word would
   otherwise escape). trig sets rep_active = 1, rp = 1 next cycle. The T word itself still goes in
   through the normal accept/bypass path, so the first loop iteration of every later
   instance of the same loop is also served.
4. Replay: while rep_active, `accept` (and the PC update) is gated off (accept = imem_ready &
   ~(v1 & stall_id) & ~rep_active) and head_present = v0 | (imem_ready & ~rep_active), so the
   stale imem bypass is never presented as valid. bacc = rep_active & ~(v1 & stall_id). The
   entry tb[rp] is a second `fresh`-like word `bfresh` that is ONLY ever stored into the queue
   (store_b = bacc), never bypassed to ID: e0 <= bfresh when (store_b & ~occ), e1 <= bfresh when
   (store_b & occ); v0/v1 update with store | store_b. rp <= tb[rp].last ? 0 : rp + 1 on bacc.
   The ID-facing head (`v0 ? e0 : fresh`), head_rs1/head_rs2, the regfile read, load-use and
   forward compares are unchanged, so the head -> regfile -> bypass -> ID/EX cone (r7s0/r8s2's
   limiter) gets no new level. In steady state v0 stays 1 and one word per cycle flows (entry
   popped and replacement pushed each cycle), i.e. no 22% imem bubbles.
   Replay start costs ~1 bubble (first replay word lands in e0 one cycle after T): 17.4k starts
   * 1 = ~0.4% of cycles.
5. Exit: the only exit is `redirect` (EX/MEM.redir, already the registered mispredict/JALR
   recovery): it clears v0/v1 as today and also clears rep_active and rec_on, and pc <=
   redirect_target as today (pc is stale during replay but is always reloaded by that redirect).
   Replayed branches carry the recorded pred bit, so EX's existing 1-bit actual_dir ^ pred_taken
   check validates them; the loop-exit is a normal mispredict (same cost as the BHT's loop-exit
   miss). BHT training from EX/MEM is unchanged and keeps running during replay.
6. Keep tb entries consistent with rvfi: pc/instr/pred come straight from the recorded
   fetched words, so pc_rdata/pc_wdata continuity and rvfi_order are preserved.

Cycle budget: 46.6% of instructions move from 1.28 to ~1.0 front-end cycles each = ~380k cycles
gross (9.4% of 4.05M); minus ~17k replay-start bubbles and partial overlap with back-end stalls
the queue already hides, so net ~6-8% fewer cycles at unchanged Fmax. Fmax risk (not
free): +~1 LUT4 on the pc enable (accept) and head_present cones, 2 extra D-input legs on e0/e1,
and ~400 extra LUT/FF placed in if_stage; none of it sits on the dmem BSRAM -> mem_res -> ID
critical path (16.0 ns) or the regfile -> bypass -> ID/EX cone.

Prediction, BHT and the ID-facing head mux stay untouched.

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-003-r9s2 (regression, -8.97%): A single 16-entry loop trace buffer (LUT-RAM `tb_mem`, replay words pushed only into queue entries e0/e1 via a store-only `bfresh`, `v0 ? e0 : fresh` head and regfile-read cone untouched) reached 229.44 vs r8s0's 252.05 against an ISS-modeled ~6-8% cycle cut, so the loss is almost certainly Fmax from the logic it hung on the late fetch inputs rather than from the head cone it carefully avoided (no Fmax/cycle split was recorded, so this is inferred): 32-bit `imem_data == tb_instr0`/`rec_close` and 30-bit pc equality compares feeding `trig`/`rec_start`/`rep_active`, `~rep_active` folded into the `accept`/`head_present` pc-enable terms, and `imem_data` fanned out to the LUT-RAM write port; this is the third attempt to hide the ~22% imem stall slots (r8s2 BTIB -2.78%, r9s1 I-cache +3.81%) and the only one that stayed positive added no `imem_data` compare and no new term in `accept`, so keeping replay off the head mux is not sufficient: do not add wide equality compares or extra `accept`/`head_present` terms on `imem_data`/`imem_ready`, and if a replay source is retried, validate it from registered queue/pc flops a cycle late and record Fmax and cycles separately.

title: Flat one-hot EX result: shared add/sub/compare chain, logic-op LUT and early 'other' leg merged in one AND-OR
motivation:
Cycles are at the imem floor (~4.05M, IPC ~0.78), so fitness only moves with Fmax. Reading the scored runs:
the worst path shown in the log is placement option 0 (arrival - 5.294 ns = period: r8s0 16.05 -> 93.0 MHz,
r9s0 15.19 -> 101.05 MHz), while the median that is scored comes from options 1/2 (always identical, e.g.
102.09 / 103.91). r9s0's MEM-steering pre-decode lifted option 0 by +8.7% but the scored median by only
+1.8%, i.e. the scored placements are limited by the EX cones (ID/EX.alu_b/rs1_val -> ALU -> ex_res ->
{EX/MEM.alu_result, P1 bypass -> ID/EX rs1_val/rs2_val/alu_b}, 14.8 ns / 37 cells in r8s1) rather than the
dmem-out cone. Today that EX cone is: carry chain (separate a+b, a-b, signed/unsigned a<b chains) ->
5-bit encoded `case (op)` result mux (11 legs, ~3 LUT levels, encoded select decoded behind the flop) ->
`div_op ? div_result : alu_out` mux (div_op itself an in.valid/!redirect/5-bit alu_op compare) ->
`(is_jump|is_auipc) ? ... : alu_result` mux -> `mul_lo/mul_hi` mux -> P1 bypass leg. That is 2-3 more LUT
levels after the adder than a flat one-hot AND-OR would need. Per the r7s0 lesson (pre-decode selects into
the previous stage's flops/decoder) the select/steering work should be hoisted into ID's ctrl bits.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Rebuild the EX result path as a flat, pre-decoded one-hot select with every non-ALU source folded into an
early-computed leg, touching no ports of the core and no cycle behaviour:
(1) decoder/id_stage compute and store in ctrl_t one-hot result selects: r_sum (ADD/SUB/SLT/SLTU result
from the shared adder, incl. LUI = 0 + b), r_logic (AND/OR/XOR), r_shift (SLL/SRL/SRA), r_other (JAL/JALR
link pc+4, AUIPC pc+imm, divider result), plus control bits `sub` (SUB/SLT/SLTU), `cmp_u` (SLTU), `lg1:0`
(and/or/xor select for the per-bit LUT), `sh_right`, `sh_arith`. MUL* keep the existing mul_lo / mul_hi
bits; sel_ex = !mul_lo & !mul_hi is one more decoded bit.
(2) alu.sv: ONE adder/subtractor `a + (b ^ {32{sub}}) + sub` (maps to Gowin ALU ADDSUB cells, the b^sub
folds into the cell LUT) whose carry-out / sign give slt and sltu (slt = (a[31]^b[31]) ? a[31] : sum[31]
style from the same chain, or MSB-flip trick for sltu) instead of four independent carry chains; logic ops
as one LUT4 per bit (a_i, b_i, lg1, lg0) that also yields LUI (= b) and passes through; one unified right
shifter (SLL done by bit-reversing the input and output, SRA by the arith sign bit) instead of three
barrel shifters. out = (sum & r_sum) | (logic & r_logic) | (shift & r_shift) | other, where `other` is
provided by ex_stage and has already been ANDed with r_other (flop select) off the late path.
(3) ex_stage.sv: build `other_leg` = r_jump ? pc+4 : r_auipc ? pc+imm : div_result (selects are flops, data
is early: pc/imm flops or divider result flops), AND it with its select there, and drop the
`alu_result = div_op ? div_result : alu_out` and `(is_jump|is_auipc) ? ... : alu_result` muxes from the
late side: ex_res = alu_out | other_leg. div_result is already registered so it may simply be gated by
`div_op` computed off-cone (div_op only changes the leg that is otherwise 0). alu_result_d becomes a flat
3-leg AND-OR `(ex_res & sel_ex) | (p_lo & mul_lo) | (p_hi & mul_hi)` so ex_res and the DSP outputs enter at
the last LUT level. Branch compares (rs1 vs rs2) stay in ex_stage unchanged.
Net: ~1.5-2 LUT levels (~1.2-1.8 ns) off the carry-chain -> ex_res -> {EX/MEM.alu_result, P1 bypass leg}
cone, which is the cone limiting the scored (median) placements, plus a smaller ALU (one adder, one
shifter) that eases routing pressure. ISA behaviour is bit-identical; the RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS branches in
alu.sv (DIV/MUL stand-ins on out/p_lo/p_hi) are kept consistent by routing them through the same legs.
Risk: ctrl_t grows by ~8 flops per pipeline stage it travels through (ID/EX only needed; EX/MEM copies
ctrl so strip the new fields from the EX/MEM payload if unused) and decode logic in ID grows by a few LUTs,
but that cone (instr -> decoder -> ID/EX.ctrl) is far shorter than the regfile-read cone. The next limiter
(dmem -> mem_res -> P2/regfile D) is untouched, so budget ~5% (not more).

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-001-r10s0 (regression, -5.97%): Rebuilding the EX result as a flat one-hot AND-OR over decoded `r_sum/r_slt/r_logic/r_shl/r_shr` flops (plus an early gated `other` leg for jal/auipc/div) while also merging the ALU into one 34-bit `a + (b ^ sub) + sub` adder (SLT/SLTU read from the carry-out `sum_ext[33]`), a per-bit LUT4 logic unit and one bit-reversing right shifter reached 237.00 vs r8s0's 252.05 with cycles unchanged by construction, so the loss is Fmax (no critical path was recorded, so the mechanism is inferred), most likely because the unit-sharing put new LUT levels in front of the carry chain (`b ^ sub`, sign-extended `ax/bx`, `sh_in` reversal mux on the shifter input) and moved slt/sltu from short dedicated comparators to the very end of the full chain feeding ex_res, which outweighed the 1-2 result-mux levels it saved; at the Fmax wall keep dedicated parallel ALU units (separate compare chains, separate shifters) selected by one-hot flop bits, and only share hardware when the shared unit adds no logic in front of the carry chain or barrel shifter, and test the flat one-hot select as its own change so its gain is not buried by the datapath rewrite.

title: Register file in distributed LUT-RAM (two async-read SSRAM copies, no reset array): 992 fewer flops, no 32:1 read mux, 31x fewer mem_res sinks
motivation:
Cycles are pinned near the 0.78 word/cycle imem floor and every single-cone fix since r5 has been
absorbed by the next-longest cone, so what is left is a flat ~10 ns wall of cones that all touch the
register file or its write data: (1) head_rs -> 32:1 read mux -> P1/P2 bypass -> ID/EX (worst path in
r7s0 at 16.8 ns, still within ~1 ns of the wall in r8s2), (2) BSRAM dmem_rdata -> load align -> mem_res
-> P2 bypass / regfile D (worst reported path in r8s0, r9s0 and r9s1, 7-9 cells), and (3) the placement
spread caused by 31x32 = 992 reset-capable flops with per-register write-enable decode plus two 32-bit
32:1 mux trees (~600 LUT4 and half of all FFs; FF 1948 / LUT4 4152 today). mem_res (the load-data net
that sits on the wall) currently drives 31 regfile flop D pins plus three bypass AND-OR legs, i.e. a
~35-sink net, because r8s0 moved the regfile write to MEM. The regfile is the only large structure
that is still built from reset flops: Yosys/Gowin only infers RAM16SDP4 SSRAM for arrays that have no
reset loop (that is how the BHT got lutram=8 in the early trees before its reset loop was added).
No previous slot has tried changing the storage structure of the regfile; r8s0 only removed the
bookkeeping (x0 gate, write-first, P3) around the flop array, which is exactly what makes it a clean
drop-in for SSRAM now: plain async read, single sync write, write result is not needed in the same
cycle (the MEM-stage P2 bypass covers the in-flight producer).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Rewrite rtl/reg_file.sv as two identical 32x32 memories (rf_a feeds rs1_data, rf_b feeds rs2_data) with
NO reset loop and combinational read `rs1_data = rf_a[rs1_addr]`, `rs2_data = rf_b[rs2_addr]`, one
synchronous write port written identically into both copies. Yosys synth_gowin maps each copy to
16 RAM16SDP4 (4-bit x 16-deep SSRAM cells, 2 depth halves, one MUX2 on addr[4]); total ~32 SSRAM cells
+ ~64 mux LUTs replace 992 FFs, 31 write-enable decoders and two 32:1 mux trees. Expected: FF ~1950 ->
~950, LUT4 ~4150 -> ~3500; the read path becomes address -> SSRAM read -> 1 mux level (vs. a 3-4 level
mux tree), and the mem_res / ex-side write-data net fans out to 4 DI pins per bit (2 copies x 2 depth
halves) instead of 31 flop D pins, shortening the BSRAM -> align -> mem_res route that has been the
reported worst path for three rounds; the smaller, less spread design also tightens placement for the
median-of-3 Fmax score.
Semantics are unchanged: SSRAM write is synchronous at the clock edge and the read is asynchronous on
the pre-edge contents, exactly the flop-array behaviour core.sv relies on (instruction in MEM writes
at end of cycle t, ID reads the new value from cycle t+1, same-cycle consumer uses P2). Because the
array no longer has a reset, x0 is made a real RAM word that is forced to zero by a reset-time write:
we = (w_en && w_addr != 0) | reset, waddr = reset ? 0 : w_addr, wdata = reset ? 0 : w_data (the AND on
wdata is the only logic added on the write-data cone and sits at the RAM DI pin, behind none of the
bypass muxes); w_addr == 0 writes are still dropped so the unit tests / formal `reg` check keep x0 == 0.
Registers x1..x31 power up as 0 on the FPGA (SSRAM INIT default) and in Verilator (zero-fill; add an
`ifndef SYNTHESIS` zero-fill initial loop for the simulation build so cosim stays deterministic; the
loop must not be visible to synthesis, otherwise Yosys may refuse the LUTRAM mapping). riscv-formal
treats unwritten registers as unconstrained and tracks only written ones, so dropping the reset clear
is fine; x0 is covered by the reset write because the wrapper asserts reset in cycle 0 (the same

title: XOR-hashed BHT index (pc[8:2]^pc[15:9]) plus 4-entry fetch-side return stack for jalr x0,0(x1)
motivation:
I replayed the real CoreMark retirement trace (2,937,037 instructions, 532,346 conditional
branches, 263 static branch sites, 49,628 JAL, 13,794 JALR) through the ISS and modeled the
current predictor offline. The 128-entry agree-BHT indexed by pc[8:2] alone mispredicts
49,400 branches (9.3%); with the registered redirect each mispredict/JALR costs about 3 or
more cycles, so (49.4k + 13.8k) redirects are ~4.7% of the ~4.05M cycles, and almost all of
the ~280k cycles above the 0.78 word/cycle imem floor. Measured alternatives:
* gshare with 2..8 history bits is WORSE than the current bimodal-agree table (41k-60k
  mispredicts), and per-branch local-history tables are no better (49k-66k), so history
  based predictors are not worth their muxes on this workload; the earlier "gshare" idea
  is rejected by this measurement.
* The loss is aliasing, not history: 263 static branch sites collide in pc[8:2]. A plain
  256-entry table gives 39,973 mispredicts (-19%), 4096 entries only 39,814, and a table
  that stays at 128 entries but is indexed with pc[8:2] ^ pc[15:9] gives 40,335
  (-18.3%, 9.1k fewer mispredicts) with NO added storage; pc[8:2]^pc[16:10] gives 40,629,
  while pc[11:5]-style hashes (>>9, >>12) give nothing (49.2k), so the fold must use bits
  [15:9] or [16:10].
* A 8-deep return stack predicts 13,772 of the 13,794 JALRs correctly (99.8%).
Together these remove about 9.1k conditional mispredicts + ~13.8k JALR redirects, i.e.
~22.9k of ~63k redirects (36%), worth roughly 1.6-2.3% of cycles. That is below the 4.6%
merge margin on cycles alone, so this is a low-risk, low-cost predictor refinement whose
value depends on Fmax staying flat; it is honest about its size rather than claiming more.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Keep the decode-in-fetch structure, the EX 1-bit direction check, the registered redirect
and the fetch queue untouched. Two small changes inside if_stage plus a carried field:
(1) BHT index hash. Replace bht[pc[8:2]] with bht[bidx(pc)] where
bidx(pc) = pc[8:2] ^ pc[15:9] (7 XOR LUTs on pc flop outputs; no extra storage, no
imem_data involvement). Training uses the same function on ex_mem.pc (pass pc[15:2]
instead of pc[8:2] as bht_upd_idx source; core.sv computes the hash or if_stage does).
Reset init (2'b10 = agree) and the agree encoding are unchanged, so cold/aliased entries
still fall back to backward-taken / forward-not-taken.
(2) 4-entry return-address stack in if_stage (30-bit entries, flops, shifted on push/pop).
Push pc+4 when the fetched word is JAL/JALR with rd == x1 (opcode and rd narrow compare,
no 32-bit equality). Predict a JALR with rd == x0 and rs1 == x1 (15-bit opcode/rd/rs1
compare, imm ignored) to ras_top: next_pc = pred_raw ? pred_target : (is_ret ? ras_top :
pc + 4). is_ret is only a select on the pc+4 leg, which is not the late leg (the
30-bit pred_target adder behind imem_data is), so the pc D cone does not gain a level on
its critical branch; the redirect mux stays last. The predicted target is carried in the
ID/EX payload (one 30-bit field + a 1-bit pred_ret that reuses pred_taken's slot) and EX
validates it with jalr_sum[31:2] == pred_target[31:2], capturing the mismatch into the
existing registered `redir` flop (redir_nxt = (is_jalr && !(pred_ret && match)) || ...), so
a correctly predicted return costs zero bubbles and a wrong one costs the same 3 cycles
it costs now. RAS updates happen at fetch accept time only (not speculative-repaired);
wrong-path pushes/pops can corrupt it but a 99.8% hit rate in the trace suggests it is
rarely an issue, and any corruption is caught by the EX target compare (correctness is
preserved; only performance is affected). If the RAS compare turns out to lengthen the
critical path, the implementer should drop part (2) and ship part (1) alone, which has
zero timing footprint beyond one XOR level ahead of the BHT read mux.

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-003-r10s2 (regression, -9.66%): Bundling a `pc[8:2]^pc[15:9]` BHT index hash (read and training) with a 4-entry fetch-side return stack (`is_ret`/`is_call` decoded from `imem_data` gating `ras_push/ras_pop` on `accept & ~redirect` into 120 RAS flops, a 30-bit `pred_target` carried through fq/IF-ID/ID-EX and a 30-bit `rs1[31:2] == pred_target` compare folded into `redir_nxt`) reached 227.70 vs r8s0's 252.05 against a ~+2% prediction whose offline-modeled cycle ceiling was only ~1.6-2.3% (hash ~9.1k fewer mispredicts, returns ~13.8k fewer redirects), so a ~10% loss can only be Fmax (no Fmax/cycle split or critical path was recorded, so the culprit is inferred) and, since the RAS-alone r5s2 was neutral (+0.09%), most likely the added XOR level in front of the 128-entry BHT read mux -> `ctr_hi` -> `pred_raw` -> next_pc cone and/or the new `pred_target`/`ret_hit` cones rather than the stack itself; an XOR on pc flops is not timing-free when it feeds that late read-mux -> pc D cone, and a predictor tweak capped at ~2% of cycles must be built and timed as separable single changes (the hypothesis told the implementer to drop the RAS if timing slipped, but nothing was measured), because on the current wall any one extra LUT level costs several percent of fitness.

title: Late-leg load bypass: dmem_rdata enters ID/EX and regfile D at the last LUT level via EX-precomputed one-hot lane/sign selects
motivation:
The champion's worst path (r8s0: dmem BSRAM -> cpu/u_mem -> cpu/u_id/reg_q.rs2_val,
8 cells, 16.05 ns arrival; r9s0 and r9s1 show the same BSRAM -> u_mem -> u_id
family still on top at 7-9 cells) is the dmem read -> lane shift / width /
sext / mem_to_reg mux -> P2 bypass mux -> ID/EX rs1_val / rs2_val / alu_b
D pin. dmem_rdata is the latest-arriving signal in the core (BSRAM
clock-to-out) but the LUT mapper treats it like any other input, so it sits
at the FRONT of a 3-4 LUT chain while the legs it is merged with (EX result,
regfile data, immediate, and the p1/p2 compare selects) all arrive earlier
and have slack. r9s0 pre-decoded the MEM steering into flops but kept
mem_res as one shared mux output with ~34 loads (three ID/EX leaves plus
31 regfile D pins) and left the P2 select as a separate level after it, so
it only gained +1.8% (7 cells vs 8). Nothing in that attempt put the BSRAM
bytes at the last LUT level, and nothing separated the regfile-D fanout from
the bypass leaves.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Restructure the load path so dmem_rdata is combined only in the last one
or two LUT levels before each flop D pin, and decouple the regfile write
net from the ID bypass leaves:
(1) EX computes, from rs1[1:0] + imm[1:0] (a 2-bit add), in.ctrl.mem_width,
    mem_sext and the misalign condition, one-hot EX/MEM flops: ld_l0..ld_l3
    (which byte lane feeds result bits [7:0]; ld_l0 also covers LW/LH@0
    bits [7:0]), ld_h1 / ld_h3 (lane feeding bits [15:8]: byte lane 1 for
    LW/LH@0, byte lane 3 for LH@2), ld_w (bits [31:16] come straight from
    rdata[31:16]), and sgn_k (k=0..3: sign source is rdata[8k+7], already
    ANDed with mem_sext and with the width that makes bits above it
    extension bits). Misalign is folded in (all zero, reg_write cleared),
    so no maddr compare remains in MEM. They are held with the rest of
    EX/MEM on dmem stall.
(2) The ID bypass does not consume a pre-merged `mem_res`. For the P2 leg
    of rs1_val / rs2_val / alu_b the final D is an explicit flat form
    D[i] = early[i] | (q_l0 & rdata[i]) | (q_l1 & rdata[i+8]) | ...,
    where q_x = (p2 hit & !p1 hit [& !alu_src for alu_b]) & ld_x is
    computed from early signals (compare outputs and EX/MEM flops) and
    early[i] is the OR of the P1 / EX/MEM.alu_result (non-load) /
    regfile / immediate legs. Upper bits [31:16] use rdata[i] gated by
    ld_w plus a shared sign net sgn = OR_k(sgn_k & rdata[8k+7]) built with
    two LUT levels from the BSRAM and fanned out to the last-level LUTs of
    the extension bits. Bits [15:8] get their own sign term as well.
(3) The regfile write data gets its own copy of the load-extract logic
    (distinct wires; keep attribute / differently ordered AND-OR so the
    mapper does not merge it into the bypass copy), so the 31-flop D
    fanout net no longer shares a driver with the three ID/EX leaves.
    Regfile enables and addresses are unchanged. If the duplicate costs
    more LUTs than it is worth or gets merged, drop (3) and keep (1)+(2).
Expected: the BSRAM -> ID/EX path drops by about two LUT levels
(~1.5-1.8 ns of the ~16 ns wall) while the P1/regfile legs are unchanged
and there is no cycle change (same hazard rules, same bubble count); part
of the gain is absorbed by the neighbouring EX ALU -> ex_res -> P1 and
head-mux -> regfile-read cones, hence the modest estimate. RVFI behaviour
is bit-identical (mem_wb fields are filled from the same architectural
values); formal ALTOPS builds are unaffected because only the load path
changes. Cocotb/cosim/formal must still pass for LB/LBU/LH/LHU/LW at all
offsets and for misaligned accesses.

implementation_notes:
# Late-leg load bypass (r11s0) — implementation notes

## What changed
* `core_pkg.sv`: new `ld_sel_t` (13 one-hot flops: `l0..l3`, `h1`, `h3`, `w`,
  `sg0..sg3`, `sb1`, `sb3`) and two new `ex_mem_t` fields: `ld`, `misalign`.
* `ex_stage.sv`: computes `ma = rs1[1:0] + imm[1:0]` (2-bit add) and from it
  the mem misalign condition and the one-hot selects. Misalign is folded into
  the captured ctrl (`reg_write = 0`, `is_illegal = 1`) and into a registered
  `misalign` flag; a misaligned/non-load gets all-zero selects. Held on dmem
  stall / cleared on bubble with the rest of EX/MEM.
  * l_k (k=0..3): byte lane k feeds result[7:0] (l0 = byte@0/half@0/word@0).
  * h1: half@0 / word@0 -> result[15:8] = lane 1; h3: half@2 -> lane 3.
  * w: word -> result[31:16] = rdata[31:16].
  * sg_k: sext and the access ends at byte k (LB@k, LH@0 -> sg1, LH@2 -> sg3)
    -> sign source rdata[8k+7] for result[31:16].
  * sb_k: LB sext only -> sign for result[15:8]. (sb0 == sg0, sb2 == sg2, so
    only sb1 / sb3 are separate flops.)
* `mem_stage.sv`: no shifter / width / sext / misalign compare. dmem_wen/ren,
  aligned mem_addr, rmask/wmask use the `misalign` flop; `mem_res_en` is just
  `ctrl.reg_write`. New output `mem_res_rf` = (`alu_result & !mem_to_reg`) |
  flat load extraction; it drives only the regfile `w_data` (and the MEM/WB
  `read_data` for RVFI). Its AND-OR is grouped differently (lanes 0/2 and
  1/3, sign nets with a different order) from the ID bypass copy.
* `id_stage.sv`: no `mem_res` input any more. rs1_val / rs2_val / alu_b are
  three instances of one flat form (generate loop `g_leaf`):
  `D = early | q&lane&rdata ... | sign nets`, where `early` is the OR of the
  P1 (ex_res), P2 non-load (`mem_alu & !mem_is_ld`), regfile and (alu_b) imm
  legs, and `q` = leaf takes P2 (`!p1 & p2 [& !alu_src]`). All `q_x = q & ld.x`
  come from compare outputs and EX/MEM flops, so raw `dmem_rdata` is the
  last-arriving input (2 LUT levels for any bit: pair AND-ORs, then OR with
  `early`). Bits [31:16] use rdata[i] gated by `q_w` plus a shared sign net;
  bits [15:8] use `q_h1/q_h3` lanes plus their own byte-sign net.
* `core.sv`: routes `io_dmemRData`, `ex_mem_w.alu_result`, `.ctrl.mem_to_reg`,
  `.ld` to id_stage; regfile `w_data = mem_res_rf`. Hazard / forward units,
  `w_en` / `w_addr` unchanged.

## Deviations
* sb1/sb3 flops added (bits [15:8] need a sign term that differs from
  the [31:16] one for LH, otherwise LH@0 sext would smear rdata[15] into
  bits [14:8]).
* The regfile copy is kept distinct only by grouping/ordering (no synthesis
  attribute); whether the mapper keeps them separate is not controllable
  from RTL. If timing shows it merged / worse, (3) can be dropped by feeding
  `mem_res_rf` from the same expression.
* Misalign trap now decided in EX (not MEM). Architecturally identical:
  RVFI trap / rd_wen / dmem gating all see the same values one stage earlier.
  `ex_res_en` (P1) is unchanged (a misaligned load in EX still raises a P1
  hit but its consumer is bubbled by the load-use rule as before).
* No new files; test_pipeline.py source list is unchanged.

## Status
* `verilator --lint-only -Wall`: clean.

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-001-r11s0 (regression, -8.71%): Pushing the dmem load extract out of mem_stage and into the three ID/EX bypass leaves (rs1_val/rs2_val/alu_b each rebuilt as `early | q_lane & dmem_rdata | shared sign net`, 13 one-hot lane/sign flops added to EX/MEM, misalign moved into EX, plus a separately-grouped `mem_res_rf` copy for the regfile D pins) reached 230.10 vs r8s0's 252.05 with cycles unchanged by construction, so the loss is Fmax (`make timing` never finished in the implementer's budget, so no critical path was seen and the mechanism is inferred), most likely because the raw BSRAM bytes now fan out to ~4 duplicated lane/sign AND-OR trees (3 leaves + regfile copy, each bit feeding up to 4 lane terms and the sign nets) so the late BSRAM output pays routing/fanout delay and extra LUTs that outweigh the 1-2 LUT levels saved, and the mapper is free to re-merge or restructure the hand-ordered "last level" anyway; this is the second MEM-load-path rewrite after r9s0 (+1.78%) and it was worse, so treat that path as exhausted by LUT-level tricks, never duplicate the load-extract per consumer, and if retried run `make timing` first (or drop the regfile-copy/(3) and per-leaf copies) and record the BSRAM-output fanout alongside the endpoint.

title: Short-cone stall-filler I-cache: 2048-word BSRAM cache, 7-bit tag, lookahead read address off the pc/BHT cone, index-verified hit
motivation:
Cycles are the one unexploited dimension. The champion (r8s0) runs 4,050,390 cycles / 10 iterations,
i.e. CPI ~1.39 on 2.92M retired instructions, against a back-end-only CPI of ~1.2: the 22% io_imemReady
stalls cap fetch at 0.78 words/cycle and every single-cone Fmax trim since r6 has been absorbed by the
next-longest path (r9s0 +1.8%, r8s1 and r6s0/r6s1 under the 4.6% margin). The only change that has ever
moved cycles past the imem floor is r9s1's stall-filler I-cache: it measured 3,586,172 cycles
(-11.5%, CPI 1.227, essentially the back-end floor) but scored only 261.66 (+3.81%, under the 4.6%
margin) because median Fmax came in at 93.8 MHz vs 102.1. The Fmax seeds were [95.1, 93.8, 93.8] and the
reported worst path was still the unchanged dmem BSRAM -> mem_res -> ID bypass path (15.81 ns arrival vs
16.05 ns in the champion), so the cache's own cones were never the logged worst path; they cost placement
quality, not a new wall. The cache in r9s1 added the heaviest possible loads on that run: the BSRAM read
address was the pc-flop D input (the full redirect > pred_target adder > BHT/pred_raw > accept cone, plus
the BSRAM-output hit compare inside `accept`), a 19-bit tag compare behind a ~2000-word x 21-bit sideband,
and 9 BSRAM blocks (vs 4) pulling the if_stage/ID logic around. This proposal keeps the measured -11.5%
cycle win and removes each of those costs, so that even a modest Fmax recovery (>= ~95 MHz at -10% cycles)
clears the 4.6% margin, and ~100 MHz gives +10%.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Re-implement the stall-filler I-cache (it fills the 2-entry fetch queue when io_imemReady = 0; it never
feeds `head`, `imem_data`, the decode-in-fetch cone or the regfile-read cone) with four timing-driven
changes versus r9s1. Everything outside if_stage.sv and a new icache.sv stays as is.

1. Lookahead read address OFF the pc/BHT cone. The BSRAM read address is not the pc-flop D input. It is
     L = (imem_ready | chit) ? pc+4 : pc          (only the 11-bit index: (pc[12:2]+1) or pc[12:2])
   i.e. a 2:1 mux of two flop-sourced 11-bit values selected by one early signal (imem_ready is a flop
   output of bench_stall_gen) and the hit term. No pred_raw / pred_target / BHT read / redirect mux sits in
   front of the BSRAM address pin. L is a *guess* of next-cycle pc (right for sequential flow and for
   back-to-back stall slots; wrong after a predicted-taken branch, a redirect, or a held pc), so the guess is
   verified, not trusted: an 11-bit flop `rd_idx_q <= L` is kept and a hit requires
   `rd_idx_q == pc[12:2]` (flop-to-flop compare, early) in addition to the tag compare. Correctness is by
   construction for any L. Cost: the first word after a taken branch/redirect is not cache-served if it
   stalls (~10% of the raw hit slots, ~1-1.5% cycles); everything else keeps r9s1's hit behaviour.

2. Tiny tag, one sideband bit, 5 BSRAM blocks instead of 9. Cache = 2048 words, index pc[12:2]. Data array
   2048x32 (4 blocks). Sideband array 2048x8 = {ok, tag[6:0]} (1 block) with tag = pc[19:13] and
   ok = valid & ~(is_jal | is_br), computed once at fill time from the existing is_jal / is_br signals
   (control words are never served: a taken B/JAL needs the decode-in-fetch steering that stays on
   imem_data only). The CLAUDE.md invariant 6 bounds all addresses to < 1 MB, so pc[31:20] != 0 simply
   disables the cache (`pc_hi_zero = ~|pc[31:20]`, flop-only): such a pc never hits and never fills, which
   keeps the cache transparent over the whole 32-bit pc space (formal/riscv-formal stay semantically
   identical to no cache). The hit is chit = ok_q & (tag_q == pc[19:13]) & (rd_idx_q == pc[12:2]) &
   pc_hi_zero & ~sweeping: two LUT levels after the BSRAM output.

3. Collision-free fill off the same imem word. Write port: WE = imem_ready & pc_hi_zero & ~sweeping,
   address pc[12:2], data imem_data (data array) and {~(is_jal|is_br), pc[19:13]} (sideband). A fill happens
   for every delivered word regardless of `accept` (the word at pc is valid whenever imem_ready = 1), so WE
   has no stall_id / hazard term. When WE = 1 the read address is L = pc+4, so read index != write index
   and the read-during-write behaviour of the BSRAM is never exercised. Use the standard one-write /
   one-read inferred RAM (Gowin SDPB), synchronous read, read enable always on, no output register.
   Post-reset invalidation: an 11-bit sweep counter writes {ok=0, tag=0} to every sideband index for
   2048 cycles after reset (outside the CoreMark start/stop MMIO markers; the BMC depth is far below 2048,
   so formal sees `sweeping = 1`, chit = 0 and the original fetch behaviour). During the sweep the sideband
   write port is muxed to (cnt, 0) and fills are suppressed.

4. Queue integration exactly as r9s1 (which passed cosim and formal), expressed on the unchanged r8s0
   fetch queue:
     use_cache = ~imem_ready & chit
     accept    = (imem_ready | use_cache) & ~(v1 & stall_id)
     store     = accept & (v0 | stall_id | ~imem_ready)       // a cache word is never bypassed to ID
     fresh_q   = imem_ready ? {pc[31:2], imem_data, pred_raw} : {pc[31:2], cache_dout, 1'b0}
     e0 / e1 D inputs take fresh_q; the ID-facing `head = v0 ? e0 : fresh` is untouched (still the pure
     imem `fresh` word), as are head_rs1/head_rs2, head_present = v0 | imem_ready, emit/NOP logic and
     redirect priority (redirect clears v0/v1 and reloads pc as today).
     next_pc   = (pred_raw & imem_ready) ? pred_target : pc + 4   // cache words are non-control, pred = 0
   The wrong-path/aliasing hazards are covered by the full-pc check (rd_idx_q + tag + pc_hi_zero), static
   code (CoreMark and selftest never write instruction memory; r9s1 passed cosim with no invalidation).

Why this should land better than r9s1: cycles are expected to stay ~ -10% (3.60-3.65M vs 4.05M) while the
new logic is shallower everywhere that mattered: no new term in the pc D / BSRAM-address cone from
imem_data -> pred_target, a 7-bit instead of 19-bit tag compare, 5 instead of 9 BSRAM blocks (less
placement pull), no write-side hazard term. The only late-ish new cone is BSRAM out -> 2 LUT levels ->
accept/store/v0/v1/CE of e0,e1,pc (it was present in r9s1 too and was not the logged worst path).
Estimated fitness: cycles x0.90 with median Fmax 95-102 MHz = 252 x (1.11) x (0.93..1.0) = 260-280
(+3% .. +11%); the 4.6% margin needs Fmax >= ~95 MHz.

Implementation and measurement notes: (a) record per-seed Fmax, cycles and the worst path, separately, in
implementation_notes so the Fmax/cycle split is known; (b) if the BSRAM-out -> chit -> accept cone becomes
the logged worst path, first drop `chit` from the address select (L = imem_ready ? pc+4 : pc, losing only
back-to-back stall hits) before touching anything else; (c) do not add any logic on imem_data other than
the fill write port and the existing decode, and no extra term on `head`; (d) keep the cache module's RAM
arrays free of reset and `initial` blocks (the sweep does the invalidation) so riscv-formal does not see a
memory with initial contents.

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-002-r11s1 (regression, +0.60%): Re-implementing the stall-filler I-cache with every cost r9s1 was blamed for removed (5 BSRAM blocks instead of 9, 7-bit tag + one `ok` sideband bit, read index `(imem_ready | chit) ? pc[12:2]+1 : pc[12:2]` taken off the pc/BHT cone and verified by an `rd_idx_q == pc[12:2]` compare, fill off `imem_ready` with no `accept` term) reached only 253.57 vs r8s0's 252.05, worse than r9s1's 261.66, so the r9s1 shortfall was not tag width, BSRAM count or the pc-D-input address cone (no Fmax/cycle split or critical path was recorded, so the cause is inferred): the lookahead guess forfeits the first stall slot after every taken branch/redirect and, as written, feeds `chit` (BSRAM output -> tag/index compare) back into the BSRAM address mux, a BSRAM-out -> LUT -> BSRAM-address loop the hypothesis itself flagged as the first thing to drop; this is the second I-cache variant under the ~4.6% margin and the narrower one was worse, so stop re-tuning the cache's address/tag cones, and only retry a stall-filler if the read address is flop-only (no `chit` term), it is measured with Fmax and cycles recorded separately, and `make timing` is read before assuming the cache's cones are off the wall.

title: Fetch-ahead cache filler that also predicts: flop-addressed BSRAM word cache feeds the queue (incl. B/JAL words via duplicated decode-in-fetch + agree-BHT) on imem stalls
motivation:
Pure direction/target predictor work is capped: cycles are 4.05M for ~3.0M retired instructions (IPC ~0.74)
against a fetch floor of ~3.85M (imem_ready is low 22% of cycles, one 32-bit word per cycle), so everything
a predictor can still remove (mispredicts, JALR redirects) is <= ~5% of cycles, and every predictor tweak
of the last rounds (RAS r5s2 +0.09%, XOR-hash+RAS r10s2 -9.66%, BTIB r8s2 -2.78%) was eaten by Fmax noise
or a new LUT level on the late fetch cone. The one lever in the fetch domain that actually moved cycles is
r9s1's stall-filler I-cache: 4,050,390 -> 3,586,172 cycles (-11.5%), but it only reached 261.66 vs 252.05
(+3.81%, under the 4.6% margin) because Fmax fell 102.1 -> 93.8 MHz. That is a ~13% cycle gain minus ~8%
Fmax, so the remaining job is (a) convert the stall slots r9s1 left on the table and (b) take the Fmax
cost out. Two concrete leaks in r9s1: it refused to fill control words (B/JAL, ~15-20% of fetched words,
because their next PC needs decode-in-fetch on the cached word), so on a stalled slot in front of a
branch the core still starves; and it addressed the cache from the late next_pc cone
(imem_data -> imm_sel -> 30-bit adder -> next_pc -> BSRAM address), stacking the cache on the most
critical fetch path. Once stalls are filled, redirects (~2-3% of instructions x 3 cycles) and the BHT
quality are a larger share of what is left, so predicting through filled words matters more than before.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add rtl/icache.sv (instantiated from rtl/if_stage.sv): 2048-word direct-mapped cache in BSRAM
(data 2048x32; sideband 2048x8 = {valid, tag = pc[19:13]}; memory is bounded to [0,1MB) so a 7-bit tag is
exact for every architecturally reachable pc; wrong-path pcs only produce words that are flushed anyway).
It is filled from every word the core accepts from imem (write port driven from the registered
fresh.pc / fresh.instr that the queue already stores, never from raw imem_data) and is read only to cover
cycles where io_imemReady = 0. Three design rules, each motivated by a past failure in LESSONS.md:

1. Flop-sourced lookup address. Do NOT read at next_pc (r9s1). Read sequentially one word ahead:
   BSRAM read address = pc + 4 (a flop-fed incrementer, or a registered pc4 copy), read-enable/CE =
   `accept`, so the output register always holds the cache word for the current pc whenever the last
   accepted word fell through (not predicted-taken, no redirect). A 1-bit flop `ahead_ok` (set on
   accept & ~pred_raw & ~redirect, cleared on redirect / predicted-taken accept) says the dout belongs to pc.
   Predicted-taken targets and redirect targets simply have no filler for one cycle (they are ~10% of
   fetches), which removes the imem_data -> adder -> next_pc -> BSRAM-address path from the cache.
2. Filler goes into the queue flops, not into the head mux or imem_data. On a cycle with
   imem_ready = 0 and hit = ahead_ok & valid & (tag == pc[19:13]) (7-bit compare off BSRAM sideband dout
   and pc flops), the cached word enters through a separate `fill` word that is muxed only into the
   e0/e1 D inputs (like r9s1's fresh_q); `head = v0 ? e0 : fresh` and `fresh.instr = imem_data`
   stay bit-for-bit unchanged (r8s2/r9s2 lesson: no new source in front of decode-in-fetch or the head mux).
   Keep `accept`'s existing imem_ready term intact and OR the filler in at the last level
   (accept_f = accept | (fill_hit & ~(v1 & stall_id))); no 32-bit or 30-bit compares anywhere.
3. Predict through filled words (the predictor part, which r9s1 excluded). Duplicate the decode-in-fetch
   cone on the cache dout: is_jal_c / is_br_c / imm_sel_c from the cached word, a second 30-bit adder
   pc + imm_sel_c (~35 LUTs), and reuse the existing agree-BHT read `ctr_hi` (indexed by pc[8:2], already
   computed) and the cached word's sign bit as `bias`: pred_raw_c = ~imm_sel_c[1] & (is_jal_c | (is_br_c & dir_c)).
   The filler's next PC is then `pred_raw_c ? pred_target_c : pc + 4`, selected only when imem_ready = 0
   (next_pc = imem_ready ? (existing expression) : filler expression). The filled word carries
   pred_taken = pred_raw_c into the queue entry's `pred` bit so EX's 1-bit direction check and BHT
   training are unchanged. The BSRAM dout and imem_data arrive at the same BSRAM clk-to-out, so the
   duplicated cone has the same depth as the existing one and only the final 2:1 next_pc mux is new.
   No other predictor structure changes (no new tables, no hash, no RAS): the BHT and training path stay as is.

Correctness/invariants: instruction memory is read-only for CoreMark (no self-modifying code; the cache is
keyed by fetch pc only), RVFI/trap/order paths are unchanged because the queue entries carry the same
{pc, instr, pred} fields, and the cache is written only from words that were really delivered by imem.
Formal: the RAM must be proven cheap in formal/run_all.sh before synth effort (r10s1 lesson) -- the
data/sideband arrays are written/read at concrete flop-derived addresses (pc+4, fresh.pc) so riscv-formal
should close, but if an `insn_*` check balloons, wrap the array in `ifdef RISCV_FORMAL` with hit tied to 0
(formal then checks the miss/imem path which is the identical logic after the queue) and report that.
Directed test: a cocotb or cosim run with a loop executed several times, with random imem_ready, must show
identical RVFI streams with and without the cache (cosim already diffs vs the Python ISS).
Expected split to record: cycles 4.05M -> ~3.45M (r9s1's 3.59M plus control-word fill ~ -3..-4%),
Fmax recovered to >= ~98 MHz because the cache address leaves the next_pc cone. Fitness ~ +6% if Fmax
holds near 98 MHz; r9s1 already proved the cycle side, so the risk is only Fmax.

changes.description: New module: 2048x32 BSRAM data array + 2048x8 {valid, pc[19:13] tag} sideband, one write port (from the queue's registered fresh pc/instr on accept) and one flop-addressed read port (address pc+4, CE = accept), dout registered; exports cached word, valid and tag.

Instantiate icache; add ahead_ok flop, 7-bit tag compare -> fill_hit; duplicate decode-in-fetch (is_jal/is_br/imm_sel, second pc+imm adder, agree-BHT dir using existing ctr_hi) on the cached word; on imem_ready=0 && fill_hit push the cached word into e0/e1 via a filler mux at the queue-flop D inputs only, advance pc to the filler's predicted next PC (last mux level after the existing next_pc), set queue entry pred bit; leave head mux, fresh.instr/imem_data path, redirect priority and BHT training untouched.
No port changes; only wire any new if_stage inputs (none expected beyond existing redirect/stall_id) so the top-level IO and RVFI shape are unchanged.

No port changes; only wire any new if_stage inputs (none expected beyond existing redirect/stall_id) so the top-level IO and RVFI shape are unchanged.

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-003-r11s2 (improvement, +13.40%): The stall-filler I-cache finally cleared the ~4.6% merge margin (285.82 vs r8s0's 252.05, after r9s1 +3.81% and r11s1 +0.60%) once the BSRAM read address was purely flop-fed (`pc + 4` with CE = `accept_f` and a 1-bit `ahead_ok` flop, no `next_pc` or `chit` term), the cached word entered only the e0/e1 D inputs via `fresh_q` with `head = v0 ? e0 : fresh` and `fresh.instr = imem_data` untouched, and B/JAL words were filled too by duplicating decode-in-fetch (second `pc + imm_sel_c` adder, existing `ctr_hi` agree-BHT) on the cache dout with `next_pc = imem_ready ? old : filler` as the only new 2:1 mux; no Fmax/cycle split or critical path was recorded, so attributing the win to Fmax recovery versus the extra control-word fill (+ ahead-read of every sequential stall slot) is inferred, but the contrast with the two weaker variants says the cache is worth its cycles only when it adds no source or late-arriving address in front of the pc D cone, imem_data or the head mux, and a stall-slot filler should cover branches and jumps rather than skip them because that is where the remaining fetch-floor cycles are.

title: Split stall_id: load-use compare off the ID/EX hold enable and the fetch accept/pc-CE cone
motivation:
The current worst path (15.9 ns, 102 MHz, 11 cells) runs u_if -> u_hazard -> u_id -> u_if, i.e.
queue head / v0 select -> load-use compare -> stall_id -> back into fetch. stall_id =
dmem_stall | load_use | div_stall is a very high fan-out net: it is the CE of every ID/EX flop
(~230), the pop/hold term of the fetch queue (v0/v1/e0/e1 next state), and the accept /
fill_acc / accept_f term that gates the pc CE, the I-cache BSRAM read enable (rd_en) and the
ahead_ok flop. The load-use term is by far its latest input (imem_data or e0 -> head mux ->
two 5-bit compares against ID/EX.rd -> AND late_res), yet for the ID/EX register it is
redundant: a load-use hazard already bubbles ID/EX through flush_id, and flush has priority
over the hold, so the hold only needs dmem_stall | div_stall. Prior lessons say single-cone
